4.3.7 Stability and convergence
The continuation or termination of the algorithm is managed by several conditions relating to
how the electron distribution 𝜓 is changing between iterations. These conditions are split into two
categories: stability and convergence, as described below.

Stability
At each step of the operator splitting method (Equation (4.38)), the 𝜓 distribution is updated
according to the CN scheme. The changes to 𝜓 during the initial few iterations are large, and then
gradually decrease until it nears the equilibrium solution, which should then be independant
of time. The condition of stability we require in this method is that the relative change in the
distribution from time step 𝑛 − 1 to 𝑛 is small – i.e. the changes in 𝜓 have begun to reduce and the
function approaches a constant value over all grid points in ̃𝑟 and 𝐸̃. The precise condition enforced
in the code depends on the method used in the algorithm, either the ‘accelerated’ method (ACC)
or the ‘constant-step-size’ (CSS) method. Both of these methods are inspired by the GALPROP
package (the relevant methods are described in the Explanatory Supplement, sec. 5.3.3 or in Strong
et al. (1998, app. B)).

ACC method In the ACC method, the initial timestep (Δ𝑡𝑖) is chosen to be large compared to the
timescales of all relevant physical effects. This value can be chosen manually in the code,
and defaults to 1 × 109 years, but should always follow the condition

Δ𝑡𝑖 > max{𝜏𝐸, 𝜏𝐷} . (4.56)

The timestep Δ𝑡 is then, from this initial value, reduced by a certain factor (the default value
in the code is 0.5) after a minimum number of iterations (𝑛min) have passed. The value
of 𝑛min can be chosen manually, and would usually benefit from some insights about the
performance of the algorithm that are gained after running benchmark tests. In the ACC
method, iterations above the cap of 𝑛min are considered to be stable. The reduction in the
value of Δ𝑡 continues until some minimum value Δ𝑡min, which defaults to 100 years in the
code.

CSS method In this method there are no hard caps on the number of iterations. Instead, we
calculate the relative difference between the 𝜓 distributions at subsequent iterations, and set
a certain tolerance threshold for this value (say, 0.1%). If the relative difference, calculated
as follows, is less than this tolerance then we consider the algorithm to be stable:

∣1 − 𝜓𝑛−1

𝜓𝑛 ∣ < tolerance . (4.57)

The ACC method is generally preferred for the majority of calculations. The primary reason
for this is that in most relevant astrophysical scenarios, there are a wide range of timescales which
affect the electron distribution. In the CSS method, using step sizes that are low enough to actually
capture the effects of shorter timescales leads to the algorithm needing a huge number of iterations
to converge on the equilibrium solution. Conversely, while needing only relatively few iterations,
large timesteps can lead to inaccurate final solutions as the impact from short-timescale processes
are lost during each iteration. The ACC method addresses both of these drawbacks, since the
timestep is changed dynamically and covers all relevant timescales (provided that Δ𝑡𝑖 and Δ𝑡min
are chosen appropriately). When dealing with various astrophysical scenarios, it could be of
benefit to tweak the parameters discussed above to find a set that leads to a convergent and
accurate final solution in the most computationally efficient way.

4.4 Method comparisons and testing
There are two main considerations when describing the accuracy of the OS method. The first is
the accuracy of the final equilibrium distribution of electrons on all relevant scales, i.e., have all
of the physical effects had the correct impact on the distribution throughout the algorithm? The
second is, how closely do the results of this numerical method compare to other solution methods,
particularly the widely-used semi-analytical methods described in Section 4.1? While aspects of
these two points have already been mentioned throughout this Chapter, we discuss them in more
detail below.

4.4.1 Accuracy and benchmarking
The accuracy of the final solution on different physical scales is directly related to the size of the
timestep Δ𝑡 and how it compares to the timescales of the diffusion and energy loss processes,

In practice, the benchmarking test described above requires a considerable number of iterations
to achieve, which takes a lot of computing time on a personal computer. While it does ensure the
most accurate solution possible when using the OS method, it is inefficient to use when there are
many computations needed (in the case of survey data being compared to many DM models, for
instance). Further, the relative difference in the electron distribution between iterations tends to
rapidly diminish at higher iteration numbers. This suggests that cutting out the final iterations that
seek the above computer-precision convergence condition can, in general, result in significantly
better computation times while having little risk of inaccuracies, which can be valuable in practical
settings. To test the accuracy of solutions found with the much more efficient ACC method, we
thus use the CSS method with the convergence condition Equation (4.59) as a benchmark test case
for a set of results. We then compare the results to those found using the ACC method, and if they
are compatible within a certain tolerance, we proceed to use the ACC method for testing various
parameter variations. The choices of either method (CSS or ACC) and whether the convergence is
based on the benchmark case are all controlled by flags in the code which allow for conveniently
switching between methods.

4.4.2 Comparisons to semi-analytical method
The second measure of accuracy we consider is how closely the solution compares to other,
independent methods. We have thus performed some basic tests of our algorithm using identical
parameters to calculations with the semi-analytical method described in Section 4.1 (referred to
from here as the Green’s Function method or GF). We first perform these calculations by using
the same GF used in Colafrancesco et al. (2015a), Beck (2019b), and Sarkis et al. (2022), and then
use a dedicated software package RX-DMFIT. The pertinent parameters used during the tests are
shown in Table 4.1, and any relevant parameters not shown therein or mentioned explicitly are
taken to be the standard values referred to at their descriptions in this thesis.

Calculations of the surface brightness for a set of targets and parameters were carried out
in Sarkis et al. (2023a), using both the OS and GF methods. We have reproduced a subset of
those results here, highlighting the most relevant comparison between methods in a galaxy cluster
scenario. In this case we observe very close agreement between the two methods, with a large
overlap in the surface brightness values for the full range of WIMP masses. The most notable
trend in these results is that for lower mass WIMPs (which produce stronger emissions, due to
the inverse mass relationship in the electron source function), there is a universal discrepancy
in the surface brightness in the inner regions of the halo. In the case of low mass WIMPs the OS
method produces slightly higher surface brightness values than the GF method in these regions,
but in all cases the OS method seems to produce relatively brighter values compared to the outer
regions of the halo. In the outer regions, there is negligible difference between the methods for
low mass WIMPs. These results seem to indicate that the most significant differences between
the two solution methods emerge from the centre of the halo. This is expected behaviour, as the
spatial dependance of the diffusive environment is retained in the OS method, but not in the GF
method.

4.4.3 RX-DMFIT
We have performed a set of simple calculations with the Radio and X-ray DMFIT (RX-DMFIT)
package, for the purpose of comparing the results to the ones obtained with the method developed
in this project. The code was originally written to extend the DMFIT package (Jeltema et al. 2008)
with radio and X-ray calculations, particularly the emissivity and flux outputs from synchrotron
and Inverse Compton (IC) processes. The code, written in C++, was obtained through an online
GitHub repository 5, which also hosts the package documentation. The information presented
in this section has been taken from either the documentation or the publication associated with
the package release (McDaniel et al. 2017). RX-DMFIT also necessarily makes use of two main
external libraries: the DarkSUSY package (Gondolo et al. 2004; Bringmann et al. 2018) and the
GNU Scientific Library (GSL) (Galassi 2009). These external tools provide the particle spectra
for the annihilation of WIMPs (necessary for the source term 𝑄) and the numerical integration
routines used for various calculations in the solution method, respectively.

Description of the code
Because of the nature of the calculations we have performed with this software, (i.e., for com-
parative purposes) we provide a brief overview of the methods used in the code and some of its
primary capabilities. Many of the concepts and methods used have already been described in this
thesis, so we will often refer to previous equations and solution techniques. The defining feature
of RX-DMFIT is that it uses the GF solution method to the diffusion-loss equation, and the method
described in McDaniel et al. (2017, sec. 2) directly follows the one introduced in Colafrancesco
et al. (2006) (also discussed above in Section 4.1). There are roughly 15 physical parameters
exposed in the code (although other hard-coded parameters could be adjusted if necessary), and
either the emissivity or the flux of synchrotron (radio) or IC (X-ray) can be computed from these
parameters at any given time. At the time of writing, calculations of the surface brightness are not
supported, so we instead use the emissivity as the primary output calculation for our comparisons.

As the code uses the GF method in the solution of the diffusion loss equation, all physical
quantities that appear in the diffusion-loss equation must be treated as spatially independant
within the Green’s functions. This is achieved as follows: the magnetic field is averaged over

below), and the gas density is given as a scalar value (equivalent to the flat profile given in
Equation (3.40)). The two options provided for the magnetic field profile, equivalent to our
definitions in Equation (3.35), are the exponential and beta profiles. There are also two supported
forms of the diffusion function 𝐷: a simple power law (given in Equation (3.21)) and a form that
incorporates the degree of uniformity in the magnetic field (Colafrancesco et al. 2006, eq. A15), as

4.5 Summary
In this Chapter we began by providing a high-level overview of some of the methods used to
solve the diffusion-loss equation found in the literature. The most common technique in DM
indirect detection studies involves the use of Green’s function approximations that are solved semi-
analytically to yield the equilibrium distribution of electrons produced duringWIMP annihilations.
One requirement of these approximations is the removal of any spatial dependance in functions
that describe physical quantities, like the magnetic field and thermal gas density profiles that
appear in the diffusion and energy-loss functions. This is usually done by averaging the relevant
profiles, and substituting the spatially-dependant functions for scalar averages in the diffusion-loss
equation.

An alternative approach to these semi-analytical methods makes use of the Crank-Nicolson
finite-difference scheme to discretise the quantities involved in the diffusion-loss equation, and then
solve it iteratively and numerically. The primary benefits of this approach are that it is significantly
faster computationally, and that the full spatial dependance of the relevant quantities can be
kept during the entire calculation. Outside a single other research team that have implemented
a numerical technique for radio DM studies, these methods are typically used in the field of
galactic cosmic-ray physics. This field has been shaped around the popular and publicly available
GALPROP code package, which has pioneered many aspects of the accurate modelling of cosmic-
ray propagation. However, the central focus of this package is on galactic cosmic-ray propagation,
and not on extragalactic DM radio studies, which is the central focus of this work. We have
therefore developed an algorithm that implements and extends the core numerical method that is
used in GALPROP, and embedded it into a general code base that contains a comprehensive suite
of DM-related calculations and models.

In this Chapter we have discussed, in detail, all relevant aspects of the developed algorithm, in-
cluding: the variable transformations used, themultidimensional extensions to the Crank-Nicolson
scheme, the specific linear algebraic techniques used to solve the related matrix equations, the
initial and boundary conditions and several important considerations relating to stability, com-
putational performance, convergence and accuracy. We have also produced a set of benchmarks
and tests of the algorithm, to ensure that the results it produces are reliable and accurate. As
part of these tests, we have carried out a simple set of comparisons to the publicly available code
package RX-DMFIT, which utilises the semi-analytical Green’s function solution method. The
overall trend in these comparisons is that there is a general agreement in the results, with certain
notable exceptions. In the centre of small structures like dSphs there can be a significant difference
in the radio emissivity output of both methods, which can in turn lead to an equally significant
difference in the total flux from these objects. As an example, we calculated the expected radio
emissivity from the Reticulum II dSph, and found a relative difference of nearly 75% between the
two methods near the centre of the halo, which led to a difference of 45% in the integrated flux
at the MeerKAT reference frequency of 1280 MHz. In the much larger Coma galaxy cluster, the
relative difference in output from the methods never went above 30%.

The differences in the predicted emissions from each method can be attributed to the mathe-
matical treatment of various modelling parameters. In particular, the substitution of the radial
magnetic field profile with a scalar average results in electrons losing less energy to synchrotron
radiation, which allows the electrons modelled by the Green’s functionmethod to diffuse outwards
from the centre of the halo a relatively further distance than equivalent electrons modelled with
the numerical method. Since this effect leads to a lower electron number density, the total radio
emissivity output from these regions is subsequently reduced. In the case of Reticulum II, the
output emissivity from the Green’s function method behaves similarly to the effect of using a
larger diffusion constant with the numerical method.

We place a large emphasis on the accuracy of the predicted emissions in the centre of DM
halos, as these are the regions where the strongest radio emissions are expected. With the recent
availability of observational data from sophisticated radio interferometers that boast extremely
high resolution and sensitivity (which is the topic of the next Chapter), accurate modelling of
radio emissions from DM on small spatial scales is essential to maximise the scientific potential
of the data. Since we use also make use of new survey data from the MeerKAT telescope in
this work, a solution method that can produce these results in a reliable and efficient way is

Observational Data

A focus point of the theoretical aspects mentioned in the above Chapters is the need for robust
modelling of the DM halo and its emissions, particularly in the dense central regions of the halo.
Correspondingly, the need for high resolution and high sensitivity radio data with which to
compare the models to is just as important. Because of the large wavelengths of the radiation in
radio studies, the spatial resolution achievable with a single radio dish is severely limited by its
physical size (which leads to giant radio dishes that are hundreds of metres wide, like the 305 m
Arecibo 1 or 500 m FAST 2 instruments). In contrast, the recent advent of radio interferometry
observatories has allowed for much higher resolutions and sensitivities to length scales not feasible
with single radio dishes. The capability of these telescopes to image the sky in such detail presents
us with a fortunate opportunity to hunt for signs of DM emission using the modelling tools already
described (a detailed study of radio instruments and their design principles is outside the scope
of this work, so we refer the reader to reference textbooks like Thompson et al. (2017) and Condon
et al. (2016) for more information regarding instrumentation). As such, we make use of recent
observations performed with the MeerKAT interferometer (Jonas et al. 2018) in this project, which
makes it the first analysis of MeerKAT data in the context of DM searches.

The MeerKAT instrument is currently composed of 64 radio dishes arranged in an array with
a dense 1 km-diameter core and a maximum baseline between individual dishes of 7.7 km. It
is located in the Northern Cape in South Africa, and released first-light images on the 16th July
2016 with the full array being completed in 2018. The pertinent observations to this project were
released as part of the first public Data Release (DR1) of the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy
Survey (MGCLS, (Knowles et al. 2022)), released on 11th November 2021. The following Chapter
provides an overview of the data from the MGCLS, how it is accessed and processed, and how
the models are concurrently prepared for a robust and statistical search within the data.

5.1 Data from MGCLS

The MGCLS is a radio survey observation programme performed between June 24th, 2018 and
June 16th, 2019 with MeerKAT’s L-band (900-1670 MHz) receiver. It consists of 115 galaxy clusters,
positioned between 0° and −85° Declination (DEC) and at a median redshift of 0.14. Each target
was observed for 5.5 - 9.5 hours with a minimum of 59 of MeerKAT’s 64 total radio dishes, for a
total observing time of ∼ 1000 hours. A comprehensive list of details for these observations can be
found in Knowles et al. (2022); in this work we focus on the enhanced data products for a small
selection of targets from this survey, which will be described as necessary later in this Chapter.

The full sample of clusters observed with MGCLS is made up of two general groups, the
so-called radio-selected and X-ray-selected clusters. The radio-selected group consists of 41 clusters
that have been observed in previous radio searches, and are likely to contain large diffuse radio
emissions in the form of radio halos or relics. Because of this selection criterion, the radio-selected
clusters also have relatively large masses. Since the total mass of these clusters is dominated by
DM, a large mass leads (in general) to a higher central DM density and thus stronger indirect
emissions. The remaining X-ray selected sample on the other hand is based only on clusters found
in the Meta-Catalogue of X-ray-detected Clusters (MCXC, Piffaretti et al. (2011)). This selection
has no bias to any radio emission properties.

The selection of targets to use for our analysis is based on several factors, foremost of which
is the lack of bright radio halos in the images. Since the expected synchrotron emission from
the DM halo (see Section 3.3.1) is diffuse and relatively faint, a bright source of non-thermal

5.2 Data processing

All the data used in this project is accessed from an online repository through a DOI 3 in the form
of archived FITS files for each source, Stokes parameter and resolution. We consider only the
enhanced data products, which include primary beam corrected images of the central 1.2° × 1.2°
map. The relevant files for our targets have been downloaded from this repository and extracted.
Each file contains multiple planes (datasets), consisting of: the intensity of the surface brightness
at the reference frequency (1280 MHz), the spectral index, the uncertainty associated with each of
these quantities, and the 𝜒2 values of a combined least-squares fit of the data. We note that the
uncertainty planes are measures of the statistical noise in the image, and not of the systematic
effects involved in the processing of the interferometric data. Then, the relevant planes for this
work are the intensity and its associated uncertainty, which are extracted from the cubes for further
processing. The full resolution data for the unpolarised intensity (Stokes-I) images are used in
this work. These all have synthesised beam sizes (represented by the FWHM - Full Width at Half
Maximum) of ∼ 7.5 − 8″ and RMS noise levels of ∼ 3 − 5 𝜇Jy beam−1.

Figure 5.1 is a visual representation of the first plane of each FITS data file, as downloaded
from the repository. These show the image intensities before any regions of interest are extracted
and the compact sources are subtracted. We note in these images the presence of various artefacts
(particularly in RXCJ0225, and around various bright compact emissions). These artefacts result
from the processing of the interferometric data, through various stages of the highly complex
calibration and imaging phases. We make no attempt to categorise these here, and refer the reader
to Knowles et al. (2022) for further details.

5.2.1 Selection of RoI
The enhanced product images are of an area of only 1.2° × 1.2° around the pointing coordinates,
as this is the region within which the applied primary beam corrections are reliable. However, the
good spatial resolution of the images (of the order of the beamwidth FWHM, 7.5 − 8″) means that
they still contain many pixels. This is an important factor for the statistical analysis performed in
this work, which will be discussed further below and in Chapter 6. To illustrate the effects of the
size of the region on the analysis, we consider the source RXCJ0757 as an example. The image of
this target contains ∼ 12×106 pixels in the 1.2°×1.2° region, which is a huge amount of image data.
However, since DM searches find the most benefit from observations in the high-density inner
regions of halos (where the strongest emission is expected), the pixels in the outer edges of the
image are less useful than those in the centre. Therefore, we crop each target’s image to a smaller
region that is focused on the centre of the DM halo, usually within a square of size 2.5′ × 2.5′. For
RXCJ0757, this results in a 120 × 120 pixel image, for a total number of 14.4 × 103 pixels. Whether
this size is reasonable or even optimal for each source depends on several factors, described below.

Firstly, there is an issue of correlation between individual pixels in any radio flux density image.
This is due to the nature of radio telescope observations, which have non-negligible beamwidths
within which the radiation is detected. This correlation can be complex to account for in general,
involving calculations of matrices that describe the covariance between each pixel. In this project,
following Regis et al. (2015b) and Regis et al. (2021), we make the approximation that all the
pixels within a single beamwidth (of the synthesised beam) are fully correlated with each other,
while those outside of the beamwidth are completely uncorrelated. This approximation will be
described quantitatively in Chapter 6. The effect of correlated pixels, and the above approximation,
on the size of the image is that it reduces the effective number of pixels (resolution elements)
considered statistically independent, which is a requirement of the statistical analysis we adopt.
Therefore, in all cases we consider the number of resolution elements in an image to be the total
number of distinct beamwidths, i.e. the total number of pixels divided by the number of pixels in
a single beamwidth. This calculation is then performed for each image. For the reduced image
size of 2.5′ × 2.5′ for RXCJ0757 mentioned above, the approximation leads to ∼ 377 resolution
elements, with 38 pixels per beamwidth.

5.3 Model Images
Once the data images from the MGCLS have been processed according to the above methods, the
next step of the analysis is to prepare the predicted model emissions for the statistical comparison.
These model emissions will have been generated by the computational procedure outlined in
Chapters 3 and 4 and saved in their final form as FITS files. The parameters that define each DM
halo environment (corresponding to each target in Table 5.1) are shown in Table 5.3. Additionally,
the following modelling configurations, which have been discussed in detail in previous Chapters,
are used in each simulation:

• WIMP masses in the range 10 - 1000 GeV

• Annihilation channels in the set (𝑏𝑏, 𝜇−𝜇+, 𝜏−𝜏+, 2HDM+S)

• Two DM halo density profiles, corresponding to the gNFW profile with 𝛼 = 1 and 𝛼 = 0.5

• Use of the full form of Equation (3.19) (i.e. both diffusion and energy loss effects are always

• Kolmogorov-type turbulence with a diffusion coefficient of 𝐷0 = 3.1 × 1028 cm2 s

• Use of the OS solution method

• Synchrotron radiation frequency equal to the MeerKAT reference frequency (1280 MHz)

5.3.1 Position of DM halo centre
The pointing coordinates used in the MeerKAT observations of the cluster sample have been given
in Table 5.1. These values do not necessarily point to the centre of mass of the cluster though,
where the centre of the DM halo should be located. The exact location of this central coordinate
can be determined in several ways: via lensing measurements, chosen as the peak brightness value
in X-ray observations of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) gas, or as the central coordinates of the
Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) in optical observations. However, as discussed at length in Seppi
et al. (2023), these independent measures of the cluster centre may be offset from each other, and
are expected to be offset for clusters that are not dynamically relaxed (due to late-time formation or
recent merger activity). The results of Seppi et al. (2023) show that the offset between the BCG and
the peak of the X-ray emissions, in a sample of galaxy clusters observed by the eROSITA telescope,
can be tens or hundreds of kpc. Since this offset can also be affected bymergers and AGN feedback,
the determination of the true centre of a cluster is a complicated endeavour that requires precise
observations and dedicated multi-wavelength studies, complemented by large-scale simulations
of the DM halo.

In the case of cool-core clusters – or more specifically, those which have dynamically relaxed
cores – we can be rather certain that either commonly-used measure, the X-ray brightness peak
or the BCG, is a good estimate for the centre of the DM halo. Unfortunately, when there is an
offset in these measures as described above, the high-resolution nature of the MeerKAT images
causes the RoI around these points to be entirely different (we note that in the lucky event that
neither region has artefacts or large extended emissions, there could be a negligible effect on the
final results, however this would have to be investigated on a case-by-case basis). Further, the
RoI’s around the MGCLS pointing coordinates are often completely distinct from these central
coordinate estimates, an example of which is shown for the Abell 4038 cluster in Figure 5.5. In
this case, the images display extremely different behaviour in the two regions, with one (at the
location of the peak X-ray brightness) showing bright extended emissions throughout the region,
while the other displays much a much fainter overall surface brightness. Such a large discrepancy
in the RoI’s would quite clearly lead to large differences in the final results (especially given
the imperfect nature of the current implementation of our source-subtraction procedure). This
example illustrates the general difficulty in selecting a location for the centre of the DM halo in
high-resolution images of galaxy clusters.

5.3.2 Model reprojection
The generated DM emission model, with proper central sky coordinates, is now mapped onto a
FITS image. This mapping procedure transforms the radial surface brightness values (calculated
with Equation (3.50)) into a two-dimensional space under the assumption of spherical symmetry.
The target pixel density of the output image can be set manually, and is chosen to be at least better
than the one found in the MGCLS images, i.e. ∼ 1″ per pixel. Due to the high resolution of these
images, the full model (which is calculated up to the diffusion radius of the halo) contains a huge
amount of data which is mostly made up of the outer regions of the halo. Since these regions are
useless in the analysis, we discard them and keep only pixels within a ‘cut-off’ radius from the
halo centre that is chosen to encapsulate each RoI. An example of an image generated in this way
is shown in Figure 5.6a, which shows a model calculated for 100 GeV mass WIMPs in an NFW-like
halo that is centred on the coordinates for the Abell 4038 cluster.

The form of the model in Figure 5.6a, while being a complete model of the DM emission, is
not yet ready for a full statistical comparison to the MGCLS data. The final step in this process

MGLCS image, including the pixel sizes and locations (in sky coordinates) and physical units.

CHAPTER 6

Dark Matter Hunting

In the previous Chapters, we described both the theoretical modelling of the expected DM
signal, and the processing of the observational data from various astronomical targets. In this
Chapter, we combine the results of each of these (generally referred to from here as just the model
and data respectively) in a robust statistical analysis that searches for any DM emissions in each
data image. The primary outcome of this analysis is a set of annihilation cross-section magnitudes,
calculated over a range of DM particle masses, that are excluded by non-detection of emission in
the data. These ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 curves are the standard way of constraining the DM parameter space in
DM indirect detection studies, and were discussed in terms of the current state of the literature in
Chapter 2 (seen in Figures 2.4 and 2.6). The following Sections provide an outline of the relevant
theoretical aspects involved in the statistical analysis, demonstrate how it is performed, and then
present the main results of the analysis with a concluding discussion.

6.1 Statistical framework
To directly compare the data to the models, we adopt a standard framework for hypothesis testing
that includes the use of 𝜒2 statistics and likelihood ratio tests. The methodology roughly follows
the one used in Regis et al. (2015b, sec. 5) and Regis et al. (2021, sec. 4) for the same purpose,
which is also discussed in a general context in Wall et al. (2003, ch. 6). The details of the specific
implementation used here will be described as follows.

6.1.1 Likelihood ratio tests
Firstly, we define the likelihood function ℒ𝑖, which defines the probability of the obtained data
given a certain set of model parameters (represented by the subscript 𝑖). In our analysis, since
the annihilation cross-section is treated as a free parameter, we use a simple range of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ values
to define each model while keeping all other modelling parameters constant. By comparing the
likelihoods of these models, we then find a value of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ that either best explains the data, or
conforms to some statistical constraint. One standard way to perform this comparison is through
a likelihood-ratio-test (LRT), which produces a test statistic 𝜆 as follows:

𝜆 = −2 log [ℒ𝑖/ℒmax] , (6.1)

where the likelihood function ℒmax is the maximum over any model likelihood ℒ𝑖. The form of
the ratio test in Equation (6.1) (i.e. −2 times the logarithm of the likelihood ratio) is written so as
to conform to Wilks’ Theorem (Wilks 1938; Silvey 1991, ch. 7), which states that:

Theorem 6.1 (Wilks’ Theorem) For a sample size 𝑛 that uniformly approaches ∞, and a parameter
spaceΘwhich has a subset Θ0 associated with the null hypothesis𝐻0, then, if𝐻0 is satisfied, the distribution
of 𝜆 = −2 log(Λ), where Λ is the ratio of likelihoods defined over Θ and Θ0, is, up to terms of order 1/√𝑛,
𝜒2-distributed with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in dimensionality of Θ and Θ0.

One of the requirements of Wilks’ Theorem is that the null hypothesis be true. In our analysis,
the null hypothesis represents the case where no DM emission at all is present in the data images,
which is set by the model ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ = 0 (with all alternative models having some non-zero value of
⟨𝜎𝑣⟩). In Regis et al. (2015b), a test for the detection of non-zero DM signals in six Local Group
dSphs is performed by calculating a LRT with the null hypothesis, similarly to Equation (6.1), i.e.

𝜆 = −2 log [ℒ0/ℒmax] . (6.2)

The normal distribution is closely linked to the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), which is widely-used
in many types of statistical analyses. In a general form, it can be stated as:

Theorem 6.2 (Central Limit Theorem) Given a sample of 𝑛 random, independent and identically-

The usefulness of the CLT in our analysis is that the distribution of √𝑛( ̅𝑋𝑖 − 𝜇) tends to a normal

6.3 Discussion
In this Section we outline some of the general trends that are observed in the exclusion curves
presented above, and then compare the results to relevant works in the literature. Firstly, we note
that the strength of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits, typically measured by how much of the parameter space below
the expected thermal relic value is probed by the results, can often be explained qualitatively in
terms of the DM modelling parameters and morphology of the image data. For example, we see
significant changes in the ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits when different DM halo density profiles are used. This is
expected behaviour, as higher DM densities leads to more annihilations in the same volume and
thus a larger number of electrons which are able to radiate synchrotron emission. Since the two
profiles examined here, the standard NFW profile and the gNFW profile with an index of 𝛼 = 0.5,
have contrasting DM density at the centre of the halo (see Figure 3.3), the higher relative central
density of the NFWprofile results in universally stronger limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩. This effect is made clear in
Figure 6.7, which compares the results from using both profiles in terms of individual targets and
annihilation channels. We see that RXCJ0225, RXCJ0600 and RXCJ0757 are significantly affected,
whereas A133 and A4038 are more robust to this change. While A133 and A4038 both have slightly
more massive halos than the other targets, they also noticeably have bright extended emissions in
the centre of their data images (caused by bright radio galaxies or extended structures like jets,
see for example Figure 5.5), which are missing in the other targets. These bright non-DM-related
emissions (and the resulting source-subtraction procedure) could be ‘covering’ the central regions
where the difference between the profiles is most stark, thus leaving A133 and A4038 less impacted
by changes to the central density profile.

Although the results produced from all clusters in the sample are relatively clustered, the
two that produce the most stringent upper limits on the annihilation cross-section are A4038 and
RXCJ0600, especially in the case of more shallowly-cusped halo profiles. Both of these clusters
probe a significant portion of the parameter space below the thermal relic cross-section, for any
halo profile index. In the case of RXCJ0600, almost the entire mass range would be ruled out for
annihilation in the 𝑏𝑏 channel and an NFW halo, and up to ∼ 200GeV for a gNFW halo. Given that

With observations from the full SKA project just on the horizon, a number of studies have predicted
strong prospects for using the SKA or its pathfinders for radio-based DM indirect detection (Co-

cluster search targets, with much attention going to the satellite dSph galaxies of the Milky Way.
Some studies have been performed that test specific models of DM, or investigate the general

produce ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 exclusion curves, as we have above. Of these works, we find that the results
presented here are almost always more constraining.

In Kiew et al. (2017), the authors studied the predicted DM-induced radio emission from six
galaxy cluster targets, for a very similar range of modelling parameters as those considered here.
The halos were modelled with NFW density profiles and 𝑏𝑏 and 𝜇−𝜇+ channels (the most extreme
channels in our results as well, excluding the 2HDM+Smodel), with a very similar set of magnetic
field and gas density models. However, they use the Green’s function solution method for the
diffusion-loss equation (as described in Section 4.1), a somewhat less sophisticated exclusion
framework, and a set of galaxy cluster targets (using a variety of radio flux observations mostly
at 1.4 GHz) that has no overlap with the one used here. The limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ can be seen in figure

our best results (RXCJ0600) the limits are strengthened by more than an order of magnitude.
This improvement can be generally attributed to the quality and general faintness of the radio
data, as the higher resolution of MeerKAT allows the crucial inner regions of the halo to be more
accurately probed with surface brightness measurements.

The above comparison is very similar for the work of Storm et al. (2013), which also notably
used the DMFIT software package for solutions to the diffusion-loss equation, and considered
magnetic field profiles that are weighted by the halo density profile. Again, the results presented
in this thesis significantly strengthen the ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ limits for compatible cases (i.e. excluding the
estimated effects of substructure) (Storm et al. 2013, figs. 3-6), which can be explained with similar
reasoning as before. A more recent study by the same authors, Storm et al. (2017), investigated the
potential indirect detection capabilities of the (at the time of publication) planned radio surveys
of LOFAR (van Haarlem et al. 2013), ASKAP (Johnston et al. 2008) and APERTIF (Oosterloo

observations are seen in figure 3 of Storm et al. (2017). Compared to the results shown here, there
is a small but distinct strengthening of the limits in all cases, with larger differences for the ASKAP
and APERTIF projections.

clusters. This study uses a wide range of modelling parameters, and also employs the operator
splitting method developed in this thesis (Chapter 4). When compared to the unaltered radio data

in the case of Ophiuchus, due to the less concentrated halo). However, the limits found using

suggest that there is any significant change in behaviour of the diffuse radio emission at smaller

Finally, we comment briefly on the status of these results compared to other multi-messenger
indirect detection studies in the literature. Our most constraining target case, that of RXCJ0600
with an NFW halo, rules out ≲ 800GeV WIMPs when annihilating through the 𝑏𝑏 channel. This
limit falls within the uncertainty region shown for the same channel in Regis et al. (2021, fig.
4), though is slightly above the most optimistic bound. Given that the limits presented therein
are the most constraining indirect detection limits on WIMPs to date, the results shown here
suggest that the approach taken in this work contains significant value to the field of radio-based
indirect detection. The results for RXCJ0600 are also more constraining than any results found
with gamma-rays, neutrinos or anti-protons thus far (see Figure 2.4 and cited references), and
notably rule out the proposed best-fit WIMP model associated with the Galactic Centre excess
measurements (Cholis et al. 2022). Outside our best case, the clusters A4038 and RXCJ0225
produce limits that are comparable with the strongest results from gamma-ray observations (Hoof
et al. 2020; Armand et al. 2021), with all other cases presented here (which correspond to more
shallow DM halo profiles or weaker magnetic field normalisations) being less stringent than
the current leading-edge results. Notably, many of our results rule out WIMPs with masses
below GeV, and almost all exclude those below 10 GeV. Since this is the mass range that is most
suited for collider-based detection schemes among the alternative search techniques (see ATLAS
Collaboration (2022) and Figure 2.2), improved results from future collider experiments should
provide a complementary view on the results presented here.

Conclusion

This thesis provides a comprehensive study of state-of-the-art radio-based indirect DM de-
tection searches. It includes detailed descriptions of the necessary physical modelling scenarios,
a rigorous presentation of a newly-developed algorithm to solve the diffusion-loss equation, a
showcase of observational data from the MeerKAT telescope, and a statistical search for DM
signals within radio images. The motivation for this work was based on one of the most pressing
open problems in modern physics, the nature of DM, and the recent emergence of sophisticated
radio telescopes that are able to image the sky in unprecedented detail and thus effectively hunt
for faint signatures of DM. The beginning of this thesis outlined some of the background and
historical aspects of astrophysical DM, the existence of which is suggested from strong observa-
tional evidence and motivated by theoretical extensions to the SM. A resolution to both of these
points could come from generic WIMPs, weakly-interacting particles that have the potential to
create observable signals through self-annihilation processes. The particular process we have
focused on in this work is the emission of synchrotron radiation in the radio band, which occurs
when electrons and positrons that are produced by WIMP annihilations gyrate around magnetic
fields. When there is a sufficient amount of DM, usually in the form of giant halos that encompass
compact astrophysical structures like galaxies or galaxy clusters, this synchrotron emission should
be visible to us as a region of diffuse radio emission. The premise of this work is thus to search for
these emissions by modelling all the necessary physical processes and comparing the predicted
emission to observational data of the region.

A large emphasis has been placed on the accuracy of the calculations of the expected DM-
induced synchrotron emission, as accurate models are needed when using modern, high-quality
radio data. For the modelling of DM parameters, which includes the energy spectra of annihilation
channels and the density profile of the halo, we have used the most up-to-date modelling scenarios
that are available in the literature. We obtained the spectra for all SM annihilation channels
from the most recent version of the PPPC4DMID results (Cirelli et al. 2011) (which also contain
electroweak corrections (Ciafaloni et al. 2011)), and used the spectra in Beck et al. (2023b) for the
annihilation channel in the 2HDM+S model. We have then used two halo density profiles, the
standard NFW profile and a generalised version of the NFW with a more shallow central cusp, in
all sets of results. Although the NFW profile provides excellent overall fits to the results of large
𝑁-body simulations, the small-scale regions around the centres of halos are still not well resolved
by these simulations. Given the uncertainty in the central regions and the lack of precise halo
modelling data in the literature for many galaxy cluster targets, the use of the two considered
profiles should encompass any variation in form of the density profile in these objects. We reiterate
that the density in these central regions is a salient factor in modern DM searches, as the ability
for high-resolution data to spatially resolve and isolate the strong synchrotron emissions they
produce can have a significant impact on the final constraints found, particularly in the case of
faint radio data.

The other modelling aspect we focused on in this thesis is the solution to the diffusion-loss
equation, which is a truncated form of the general cosmic-ray propagation equation that encapsu-
lates the relevant effects of diffusion and energy-loss. The equilibrium solution to this equation is
necessary for the calculation of the expected synchrotron emission from a population of electrons,
however the nature of being a second-order partial differential equation means it requires a set of
non-trivial mathematical techniques to solve. A common approach to finding these solutions in
the literature has been a semi-analytical method that makes use of Green’s functions to find the
equilibrium solution directly. This approach has two significant drawbacks for general use: it can
be computationally expensive, and it requires approximations about the spatial distribution of any
involved physical quantities (like the magnetic field or thermal gas density). In this thesis we have
therefore presented, in rigorous detail, a numerical solution method that has been developed with

Page 89 of 104



7. Conclusion M. Sarkis, PhD Thesis

the primary purpose of addressing these two drawbacks, and solving the diffusion-loss equation
in a computationally performant and accurate way. The method is based on the Crank-Nicolson
finite-differencing scheme (generalised to multiple dimensions with an operator-splitting tech-
nique) that calculates the equilibrium solution iteratively. The implementation of the algorithm
used in the method draws inspiration from the GALPROP package (Strong et al. 1998), which is
a well-developed publicly-availalble software package used extensively in the field of galactic
cosmic-ray physics.

To test the solution method developed in this project, we have provided a set of comparisons
between the results of our code and RX-DMFIT (McDaniel et al. 2017), which is another publicly-
available software package that uses a semi-analytical method to solve the diffusion-loss equation.
The package has been used in the literature to compute the expected synchrotron emissions from
DM halos, and in the results presented here we compare the output DM-induced radio emissivity
and integrated flux for a model galaxy cluster and dSph galaxy. We found general agreement
between the output of each code, with some notable exceptions. Principle among these was a
significant difference in the emissivity function at small radii within the dSph halo, with our code
leading to a maximum of 75% more emission in this region. The difference was attributed to the
mathematical treatment of the physical quantities involved, and in particular the substitution
of the full magnetic field profile with a scalar average. This approximation leads to electrons
at the centre of a DM halo losing relatively less energy to synchrotron radiation, which allows
them to diffuse further through the halo. This effect reduces the electron number density in
the inner regions of the halo, and thus also reduces the total output emission from this region.
Since the high-density central region of a halo is of such importance in searches for DM-related
emission, this lack of spatial accuracy can represent a major hindrance when using these models
in conjunction with high-resolution observational data.

Several studies have shown that the SKA and its precursor instruments, with their high
sensitivity and spatial resolution, are well-suited to produce novel DM search results, and the
first studies to utilise ASKAP and MeerKAT data have already placed stringent constraints on the
DM parameter space. In this work, we selected five nearby galaxy clusters, observed as part of
the MeerKAT Galaxy Cluster Legacy Survey programme (Knowles et al. 2022), to act as a set of
observation targets within which to hunt for radio signals of DM. These galaxy clusters are all
at a low redshift (𝑧 ≤ 0.06) and were chosen based on several criteria related to their potential
effectiveness in DM searches, such as the overall quality of the data, the amount of bright compact
emission present in the image, and the availability of modelling parameters in the literature. The
data images for the chosen targets were subject to a number of processing techniques to prepare
them for a statistical DM signal search, which included the selection of an optimal region around
the centre of the cluster (to leverage the strong emissions in these regions) and the removal of
any compact emission in a source-subtraction process (as these sources hide the relatively faint
diffuse synchrotron emission from DM). These processed images were compared to the computed
model emissions from the DM halos in each target, which were mapped onto two-dimensional
FITS images and reprojected onto the same coordinate system as the data, ensuring that each pixel
in the model image corresponded to the exact sky location of the data image.

The comparison betweenmodel and data images then followed a standard statistical framework,
using a likelihood ratio test, that resulted in a set of ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 exclusion curves calculated at
a confidence level of 95%. Of the targets considered here, the galaxy cluster RXCJ0600.8-535
produced the strongest constraints on the cross-section ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩, regardless of the density profile
used to model the DM halo. This was primarily due to the relative faintness of the region in the
radio data provided by the MGCLS, which allows for more penetrative testing of the DM model
emissions. When using an NFW density profile, there is at least partial coverage of the thermal
relic cross-section limit from all targets, with especially strong constraints on lower mass WIMPs.
When the gNFW profile is used the resulting constraints are (expectedly) weaker, particularly
for targets with faint radio data in the region of interest, although in some cases this modelling
scenario still produces constraints on low-mass WIMP models.

Our results also included a variety of representative annihilation channels that are well-studied
in the literature, like quark or leptonic channels, as well as the comparatively unexplored 2HDM+S
model. The leptonic channels (𝜇−𝜇+ especially) produce steep ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ − 𝑀𝜒 curves, providing
strong constraints on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ at low masses, whereas the quark channel (𝑏𝑏) has a flatter curve, but

7. Conclusion M. Sarkis, PhD Thesis

probes the thermal relic cross-section at larger masses. The limits on ⟨𝜎𝑣⟩ presented here are
almost always more constraining than current results (that use corresponding source targets and
modelling scenarios) in the literature. The results from the 2HDM+S channel produce relatively
weaker constraints than the SM channels, but are in general comparable to the limits found for
this model in the literature. Our exclusion curves agree with the trend in modern radio-based
DM indirect studies that rule out low-mass WIMPs, requiring remaining viable models to have
relatively higher masses, of hundreds of GeV.

Given that most of the galaxy clusters used as search targets in this work have not been used in
indirect detection studies before, these results represent a strong opening move for DM searches
in galaxy clusters with MeerKAT data. Future work in this field, which could include directed
observations from MeerKAT (rather than the survey observations used here), improved source
subtraction procedures, or more advanced analysis techniques (like interferometric data-stacking
or baseline tapering), promises to deliver even better results in the ongoing search for the nature
of DM. With observations from the full SKA on the horizon, we can also look forward to a future
with completely ruled out parameter spaces, or even the detection of a so far elusive DM signal.

Abstract

Weakly-Interacting-Massive-Particles (WIMP) provide a possible solution to the unanswered
question of the underlying nature of dark matter in the universe. In this thesis, we explore the
WIMP paradigm with different theoretical frameworks in order to get a deeper understanding
of dark matter observables, which can be tested in current and future experiments.

In order to gain further insight into the impact of experimental constraints on parameter
scans and their interplay with each other, we investigate the complex Two-Higgs Doublet
model. Here, we quantify the allowed CP-violation in the fermionic couplings to the Standard
Model-like Higgs boson. To improve our scanning procedure, we furthermore employ modern
machine learning algorithms.

Exploring the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model can
become a tedious task, due to the large number of parameters in the model. We therefore
develop the tool NMSSMScanner, which allows us to explore the parameter space in a convenient
way. As a proof-of-concept, we maximize the production cross section of a resonant non-
Standard Model-like Higgs boson decaying into various final states. Furthermore, we calculate
the dark matter relic density and direct detection cross section in this model to further
constrain the available parameter space with experimental data. To incorporate these features
into our toolchain, the dark matter code RelExt is extended by an implementation of the
calculation of the relic abundance and the direct detection cross section in this theoretical
framework.

In addition, we calculate the dark matter relic density at next-to-leading order including
electroweak and QCD corrections in the framework of the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model. We argue that the inclusion of higher-order calculations is important in
understanding the parameter space in dark matter models. This work is used as a proof-of-
concept, in order to automate the next-to-leading order relic density calculation in RelExt

for arbitrary models in future works.

Zusammenfassung

Schwach wechselwirkende massive Teilchen (engl. weakly interacting massive particles (WIMP))
können eine mögliche Antwort auf die Frage nach der zugrunde liegenden Natur von dunkler
Materie darstellen. In dieser Arbeit werden wir das sogenannte WIMP-Paradigma in ver-
schiedenen theoretischen Modellen untersuchen, um ein tieferes Verständnis der Observablen
des dunklen Materieteilchens zu gewinnen. Diese können in gegenwärtigen und zukünftigen
Experimenten getestet werden.

Um weiterführende Einblicke in die Auswirkungen experimenteller Einschränkungen auf Scans
im Parameterbereich und das Zusammenspiel der Parameter zu erhalten, werden wir das kom-
plexe Zwei-Higgs-Dublett-Modell untersuchen. Hierbei werden wir die theoretisch erlaubte
Ladungs- und Paritätsverletzung in den fermionischen Kopplungen zum Standardmodell-
Higgsteilchen quantifizieren. Dabei werden wir moderne Machine-Learning-Algorithmen zur
Verbesserung unserer Scanverfahren einsetzen.

Die Untersuchung des nichtminimalen supersymmetrischen Standardmodells kann aufgrund
der großen Anzahl an Parametern zu einer mühsamen Aufgabe werden. Wir entwickeln
deshalb ein Tool, mit dem man den Parameterraum bequem untersuchen kann. Als Proof-of-
Concept wird der Wirkungsquerschnitt für die resonante Produktion eines nicht im Standard-
modell enthaltenden Higgsbosons maximiert, welches in verschiedene Endzustände zerfällt.



viii

Des Weiteren berechnen wir in diesem Modell die Reliktdichte der dunklen Materie sowie
den Wirkungsquerschnitt für den direkten Nachweis von dunklen Materieteilchen in Streuex-
perimenten. Hierfür wird der Code RelExt erweitert, indem die Berechnung der Reliktdichte
und des Wirkungsquerschnittes für die dunkle-Materie-Streuung an Nukleonen implementiert
wird.

Darüber hinaus wird die Reliktdichte im Kontext der komplexen Singulett-Erweiterung des
Standardmodells auf nächsthöherer Ordnung berechnet. Dabei wird gezeigt, dass die Hinzu-
nahme von Korrekturen höherer Ordnung wichtig ist, um den Parameterbereich von Dunkle-
Materie-Modellen besser zu verstehen. Diese Arbeit wird als Proof-of-Concept dienen, um
in zukünftigen Arbeiten die Berechnung der Reliktdichte auf nächsthöherer Ordnung für be-
liebige Modelle in RelExt zu automatisieren.

CHAPTER 1

Introduction

The success story the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics has been underlined by the
discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 by the ATLAS [1] and CMS [2] collaborations at the Large
Hadron Collider (LHC). However, even though the SM is able to explain many phenomena,
there are questions that still remain unanswered, which indicates the existence of physics
beyond the SM (BSM).

One of these open questions is the underlying nature of dark matter in the universe. The
Standard Model of Cosmology is able to describe the evolution of the universe, while only
being dependent on some parameters, which can be obtained by the measurement of the
Cosmic Microwave Background [3]. From this measurement, we observe that ∼ 5% of the
energy budget of the universe is baryonic in nature, while ∼ 27% consists of dark matter. It
is assumed, that dark matter is electrically neutral, cold, i.e. moving at non-relativistic veloc-
ities, and collisionless, and has a lifetime longer than the age of the universe. Therefore dark
matter solely interacts through the gravitational force and couples weakly to SM particles.
The SM cannot provide a suitable dark matter candidate, thus we have to investigate BSM
frameworks.

A promising type of candidates for dark matter are Weakly-Interacting-Massive Particles
(WIMPs). The so-called WIMP-paradigm states that the experimentally measured dark
matter relic abundance, which reads [3]

Ωch
2 = 0.1200± 0.0012 , (1.1)

can be obtained with a dark matter particle with a mass and couplings to SM particles of the
order of the electroweak scale. Extensions of the SM scalar sector can provide such WIMPs.
In these Higgs portal models, the dark matter candidate communicates with the SM via a
Higgs mediator. These models have two advantages. The first advantage is that extending
the scalar sector of the SM provides us with a rich phenomenology which can be probed not
only at the LHC, but also in future collider experiments. The second advantage is that the
Higgs portal models can be probed in different and complimentary experiments in order to
discover a possible dark matter signature. In direct detection experiments, one can use the
Higgs boson as a mediator in dark matter-nucleus scattering [4]. At the time of writing this
thesis, no signal in direct detection experiments has been measured. Nonetheless, these null
results provide exclusion limits that constrain the parameter space of a given model.



2 1. Introduction

Calculating the dark matter relic abundance can become tedious when dealing with models
that include not one but multiple dark sector particles. To circumvent this issue, we have
developed a tool that computes the relic density for an arbitrary dark matter model with
a single dark matter candidate stabilized by a discrete symmetry. Additionally, we imple-
mented algorithms to explore the parameter space in which the dark matter relic abundance
agrees with the experimental measurement. In the literature, the dark matter relic density
is, in most models, calculated only with leading-order diagrams. However, as experimental
precision improves, theoretical predictions must also become more precise. Therefore, we
will investigate in this thesis the impact of next-to-leading order electroweak and quantum
chromodynamics (QCD) corrections on the dark matter relic abundance.

This thesis consists of five main parts. In Part I, we will first give an short overview of the SM
(Sec. 2.1) and proceed with establishing the different BSM frameworks, which are the Complex
Singlet Extension of the Standard Model (CxSM) (Sec. 2.2), the complex Two-Higgs Dou-
blet Model (C2HDM) (Sec. 2.3) and the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model
(Sec. 2.4). Afterwards, we will provide a short introduction into the Standard Model of Cos-
mology in Ch. 3, and thereby develop the mathematical framework to calculate the dark
matter relic abundance in Sec. 3.5 and the direct detection cross section in Sec. 3.6.

To give precise theoretical predictions, we need to understand the impact of experimental
constraints on the parameter space in a given BSM theory. Therefore in Part II, we will in-
vestigate the interplay between collider constraints and the constraints of the electric dipole
moment on the parameter space, by quantifying the allowed size of charge-parity (CP) vi-
olation in the fermionic couplings to the SM-like Higgs boson. We will first provide the
expressions in order to calculate the electric dipole moment in Sec. 4.1. Afterwards, we will
present the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and also the scan ranges of our
input parameters in Ch. 5. In order to obtain our results, we will use two different approaches.
In the first strategy, we will use a guided scan, while in the second strategy we will use ma-
chine learning algorithms in order to explore the parameter space. The results for the former
case will be presented in Ch. 6. In Ch. 7, we will give a short overview on the used machine
learning algorithm, which is succeeded by results using this technique. Finally, Ch. 8 will
conclude this part.

In Part III, we will consider the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM),
where we developed the tool NMSSMScanner.As a proof-of-concept of our new tool, we max-
imize the cross section values for the production of a Higgs boson X, which subsequently
decays into a pair consisting of a SM-like H plus non-SM-like Higgs boson Y , X → HY using
a Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo algorithm. Furthermore, the NMSSM provides a possible dark
matter candidate, which is the lightest supersymmetric particle. Therefore we provide in
Sec. 9.1, the framework how to calculate the dark matter relic abundance in the NMSSM.
Furthermore, in Sec 9.2 we provide also an overview on how the direct detection cross section
is obtained in the NMSSM. In Ch. 10, we present our dark matter tool RelExt, which is
able to compute the dark matter relic abundance, assuming the freeze-out mechanism, for an
arbitrary dark matter model where the dark matter particle is stabilized by a discrete symme-
try. We furthermore extend the code by implementing the relic density and direct detection
calculation for the NMSSM. In Ch. 11, we will present an overview of the tool NMSSMScanner,
the additional observables tested and the computer codes used in the analysis. The results
of our analysis will be presented in Ch. 12. Finally, in Ch. 13 will conclude this part.

In Part IV, we will investigate the impact of higher-order corrections on the dark matter relic
density in the framework of the CxSM. We will first present how to obtain the dark matter
relic density at next-to-leading order in Sec. 14.1. Here, ultraviolet and infrared divergences
can arise. We will present in Ch. 15 how we treat these and show how to obtain ultraviolet-
and infrared-finite annihilation cross sections. In Ch. 16, we present all relevant theoretical



3

and experimental constraints and provide the scan ranges of our parameter sample. In Ch. 17,
we will present the results of our analysis. Finally, we will conclude this part with a summary
and outlook in Ch. 18. Part V is the final part and consists of a summary and conclusion of
this thesis.

2.1. Standard Model of Particle Physics

The SM is a quantum field theory [5] that describes the fundamental particles and their inter-
actions. Unifying the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces into a single theory describes
these interactions in terms of local gauge groups. The Lagrangian of the SM is invariant

2.4. Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model

In this section, we will briefly introduce the NMSSM. Here, we will follow the reviews [45,46]
and the works of [9, 47].

The NMSSM goes beyond the minimal supersymmetric extension of the SM, the MSSM.
While in the MSSM the SM scalar sector is extended by an additional scalar doublet, the
NMSSM adds an additional scalar singlet field. Further, each field is promoted ot a superfield,
which contains both SM (and the additional scalar doublet and singlet) degrees of freedom
and the ones of their supersymmetric partner, the superpartner. These superpartner differ
from the SM particles only in their spin quantum number by 1/2. This leads to the following
particle content

• The fermions of the SM, obtain spin-0 superpartners, the sfermions. Accordingly, the
superpartners of quarks leptons are therefore called squarks and sleptons, respectively.

Brief Overview of the Standard Model of Cosmology

One of the most sought-after problems in modern physics is the existence of dark matter.
Little is known about the nature and properties of dark matter. However, there is multiple
evidence (cf. Refs. [3,50,51]). To compute and study dark matter observables, it is necessary to
first establish the theoretical framework in which these quantities can be consistently defined
and evaluated. This framework is the so-called Standard Model of Cosmology. Note that
explaining it in its full complexity is beyond the scope of this thesis. We therefore refer to
Refs. [52–54] for a more comprehensive overview. In this work, we will focus only on aspects
relevant to understanding the thermal history of the universe and to calculating dark matter
observables, in particular, the relic density. Here, we follow the description given in Ref. [53].

3.1. General Relativity

We start our description with Einstein‘s field equations (EFEs), which read

Gµν + Λgµν = 8πGTµν . (3.1)

Here, Gµν ≡ Rµν − 1

2
gµνR denotes the Einstein tensor, which represents the curvature of

space-time, Rµν is the Ricci tensor, R the Ricci scalar, G is the gravitational constant, gµν
is the metric tensor and Λ is the cosmological constant. Further, Tµν denotes the energy
momentum tensor, which reads

Tµν = (ρ+ p)uµuν + pgµν + qµuν + uµqν + πµν , (3.2)

where uµ is the velocity four-vector, ρ the energy density, p denotes the isotropic pressure, qµ
is the energy flux and πµν is the anisotropic pressure. Also, ρ, p, qµ and πµν are dependent
on space and time. In the Standard Model of Cosmology, it is assumed that the cosmic
fluid behaves as a perfect fluid, i.e., qµ = 0 and πµν = 0, corresponding to a large-scale
homogeneous and isotropic description of the universe. The energy-momentum tensor then
reduces to

Tµν = (p̄+ ρ̄)uµuν + p̄gµν . (3.3)

baryon-photon fluid as the photons decoupled from the thermal bath. During this period,
gravitational wells formed from large amounts of dark matter. These gravitational wells pull
the baryon-photon fluid inward, thereby compressing it. This process is counteracted by
the pressure exerted by the photons, which leads to a rarefaction of the fluid. The tem-
perature fluctuations of the CMB are then induced as the photons travel through different
regions with varying gravitational potentials. Through the compression and rarefaction of

the baryon-photon fluid, oscillations are created. These oscillations are embedded in the
power spectrum of the CMB, where the even-numbered peaks correspond to acoustic modes
undergoing compression at the time of photon decoupling, while the odd-numbered peaks
correspond to acoustic modes in a rarefaction phase. Through the amplitudes and positions
of the peaks, we can now extract the cosmological parameters of the ΛCDM. The position of
the first peak, which corresponds to the time of last scattering, allows us to infer the curvature
of the universe. Further, the baryon content of the universe can be examined by taking the
ratio of the amplitudes of the first and second peaks in the CMB power spectrum. This is
motivated by the fact that if a higher baryon content exists in the baryon-photon fluid, this
would result in a stronger compression and a weaker rarefaction. Vice versa, a smaller baryon
density results in weaker compression and stronger rarefaction of the fluid. Analyzing, there-
fore, the amplitude ratios of the first two peaks allows us to obtain information on the baryon
content in the universe. Furthermore, because dark matter does not interact with photons,
it would only affect the amplitudes of the compression peaks. Therefore, a large third peak

Thermal Freeze-Out

In this production mechanism, we assume that in the early Universe every particle, including
the dark matter particle, is in thermal equilibrium with the thermal bath. This implies
that the production and annihilation rates are equal. However, due to the expansion of the
Universe, two effects occur, which we briefly explain below.



28 3. Brief Overview of the Standard Model of Cosmology

1. As the Universe expands, the temperature T decreases. Consequently, light particles
no longer have enough energy to efficiently produce heavy particles. The annihilation
process then becomes dominant, and the heavy particle number density decreases.

2. Due to the expansion of the Universe, it also becomes less likely for two particles to
interact. As a result, the annihilation rate Γann decreases. When the annihilation rate
becomes comparable to the expansion rate of the Universe, i.e. Γann = H, annihilations
cease to be efficient. This point in time is referred to as freeze-out point.

CHAPTER 4

Introduction

To make predictions across different BSM models, it is important to understand how con-
straints affect the parameter space. In this part, we will investigate how collider constraints
and the electron electric dipole moment (eEDM) constraint interplay in the C2HDM frame-
work, which we introduced in Sec. 2.3.

We work in a CP-violating 2HDM with a softly broken Z2 symmetry that allows CP violation
both in the scalar potential and the Higgs Yukawa interaction. The model naturally eliminates
FCNC at tree level while still accommodating CP violation, thereby generating EDMs for
fundamental particles. The dominant contributions of the EDM are given by the two-loop
Barr-Zee diagrams [67]. Further, it has been seen in Ref. [41] that a new type of two-loop
diagrams, dubbed as ”kite diagrams”, are necessary to obtain a gauge-independent result.
In recent developments [68], it has also been shown that one-loop diagrams are relevant
to the calculation of the eEDM. There are two reasons why it is important to keep track
of the relevant diagrams when calculating the eEDM. First, the experimental sensitivity is
steadily improving: the current 90% confidence-level limit given by the ACME collaboration
is 1.1× 10−29e.cm [69–71], while the JILA collaboration sets a limit of 4.1× 10−30e.cm [71].
However, the individual contributions to the eEDM are of order 10−27. This means that
there must be a large cancellation among the eEDM diagrams to obtain a significant CP
violation, while still accommodating the eEDM constraints. In prospect of the expected
future sensitivity of O(10−33) [72–74], formerly neglected diagrams become more and more
relevant. We also show that virtual charm quarks must be considered in the Barr-Zee diagrams
to obey the expected sensitivity.

Our approach will be as follows. We will perform an extensive parameter scan in the Type
II of the C2HDM with h2 = h125, where h125 represents the SM-like Higgs boson. Here, we
apply all theoretical and experimental constraints to obtain a valid parameter set. We will
use two scan methods in our analysis, the guided scan and a scan using Machine Learning
(ML) algorithms. These scans are then used to quantify the allowed size of CP violation in
the fermionic couplings to the SM-like Higgs boson, in light of additional contributions to the
EDM calculation and the most recent experimental data.

In this chapter, we present the formulas used to compute the electron EDM. Then we will
provide the list of theoretical and experimental constraints applied, along with the scan ranges
for the input parameters.

Fermion Masses used in the EDM Calculation

An additional question, aside from which diagrams to include, arises regarding the choice of
the renormalization scheme. Explicitly, two different schemes can be employed regarding the
fermion mass renormalization. The most common renormalization schemes used for the top
and bottom masses are the MS masses evaluated at the scale µ = MZ (mt(MZ),mb(MZ))
[41, 78, 80] or the pole mass used for the top quark and the running MS bottom quark mass
evaluated at the scale µ = mb, i.e., (mt,mb(mb)) [39,81–83]. For the third generation lepton
τ , we always use the pole mass mτ . For brevity, we will refer to the first choice as MZ-
masses scheme and to the second choice as ”pole masses” scheme. In previous work [84], that
did not include the full two-loop calculation including the kite contribution in the eEDM,
it has been shown that the choice of the used renormalization scheme has an impact on the
phenomenological results. Here, in the Type-II of the C2HDM, with h2 = h125 has been
investigated. By evaluating the fermions at the MZ scale, it has been found that a sizeable
CP-odd component in hSMbb̄ is excluded by the combined experimental constraints from the
upper limit on the eEDM and from the cross-section limits searches for BSM scalars. On the
other hand, by using the pole mass scheme, the possibility of sizeable CP-odd components
remained possible. We will investigate these statements in this work in light of the updated
eEDM calculation with the additional kite contributions.

Numerical Setup of the Analysis

The goal of our analysis is to probe the CP nature of the SM-like Higgs boson. To achieve this,
we perform an extensive scan of the parameter space, constrained by all relevant theoretical
and experimental constraints. In the next section, we will briefly present all experimental
and theoretical constraints used in our analysis.

5.1. Experimental and Theoretical Constraints

5.1.1. Theoretical Constraints

In principle, one can choose the input parameters given in Eq. (2.61) freely. However, not
every combination of parameters will constitute a valid parameter point, as these parameters
must still satisfy theoretical and experimental constraints. To obtain a point, which is con-
sistent by theory, it has to fulfill the condition that the potential is bounded from below and
has a global minimum with a VEV of v = 246 GeV, such that the physics described in this
model is stable and consistent with phenomenology. Furthermore, the chosen input param-
eters must satisfy the condition of perturbative unitarity. In the next two subsections, we
discuss the conditions associated with these constraints to ensure that the parameter points
are theoretically consistent. In our analysis, these conditions are implemented and checked
for each parameter point.

5.2. Experimental Constraints

Electroweak Precision Measurements

Measurements of electroweak observables are sensitive to loop-induced effects from new
physics. If the BSM effects are captured completely by the self-energy corrections to the
gauge boson propagators, one can parametrize these effects through the oblique parameters
S, T , and U [97, 98]. To obtain a valid parameter point, we require that these agree at the
2σ level with the global fit of Ref. [99], which is given by

S = 0.04± 0.11, T = 0.09± 0.14, U = 0.02± 0.11 . (5.5)

Flavour Constraints

From the rare B-meson decays, in particular the process b→ sγ, we obtain constraints for the
charged scalar mass mH± . We incorporate this constraint using the formula from Ref. [100].
Here, we require that the result agrees with the experimental measurement at 3σ [101]. It
has been shown [102–106] that this implies a lower bound of mH± ≥ 580 GeV at 95% CL for
the Type II C2HDM. Additionally, the global fit of Ref. [99] confirms this lower bound and
also shows that this also holds for the Lepton flipped type.

In the previous chapter, we used a guided-scan method to obtain the parameters. However,
Ref. [119] shows that when using machine learning (ML) algorithms to scan the parameter
space, the traditional method often misses a large portion of the valid parameter space,
with significant consequences for phenomenological interpretations. This motivated us to use
these ML algorithms within the C2HDM framework. In general, ML has become essential for
particle physics analysis [120–124]. In particular, it has become essential for data analysis in
experiments like the LHC, as the data obtained has become more complex and the sample sizes
have grown larger. We are interested in exploring the parameter space of BSM theories. Given
the goal of discovering the unknown physical implications in a highly constrained parameter

7.1. Covariant Matrix Adaptation Evolutionary Strategy

Evolutionary strategies (ES) use an iterative process in which possible solutions to a given
problem are tested, and the best are used to generate new ones. In BSM physics, the solution
to the problem is to find valid parameter points that minimize Eq. (7.2). In contrast to
Genetic Algorithms, ES does not use a previously sampled data set to generate new points.
Instead, the new solutions are generated from a distribution called the generation. The points
for each generation are sampled from the parameter distributions based on the best candi-
dates from the previous iteration. In CMA-ES, the distribution is a multivariate normal
distribution N i(mi, Ci), where mi denotes the mean value and Ci is the covariance matrix
of the i-th generation. As stated before, we initialize the normal distribution with a random
point as its mean, and set the covariance matrix to the identity matrix multiplied by a global
factor σ. From this distribution, λ candidates are generated, and their suitability is checked
with Eq. (7.2). Afterwards, the best µ candidates are sorted and from these a new distri-
bution N i+1(mi+1, Ci+1) are generated, with a new mean mi+1 and a new covariant matrix
Ci+1. This procedure is expected to behave similarly to first- and second-order optimization
methods. The mean is updated along the direction of steepest descent of the loss function,
while the covariance matrix provides an approximation to its Hessian. However, CMA-ES
does not calculate the derivatives of the loss function, which in fact means that one can use
it on nonconvex, ill-conditioned, and non-continuous loss functions. This has the advantage
that the algorithm converges quickly and can be applied to various applications. For further
information on this strategy, we refer to Ref [125].

A major advantage of CMA-ES is the quick convergence compared to other black-box search
algorithms. The caveat of this algorithm is that the explored parameter space is highly
localized. In our approach, which was also applied in Ref. [126], we add a novelty reward
to the loss function. Here, we calculate the point density and add it to the loss function as

model parameters. Furthermore, we can penalize not only the model parameters but also
physical quantities, such as the CP-odd angle given in Eq. (5.8). This allows us to explore
not only the valid parameter space but also to find new phenomenological characteristics of
