CHAPTER 8

Conclusion

In this part of the thesis, we investigated the impact of the collider and eEDM constraints
on the parameter space of the C2HDM, which we introduced in Sec. 2.3.

We first introduced the formulas used for the full two-loop eEDM calculation, including a
new class of diagrams, the so-called kite diagrams. Furthermore, we investigated the depen-
dence on the renormalization scheme used for the fermion masses in the eEDM calculation.
Afterwards, we gave an overview of the theoretical and experimental constraints applied in
our study. In the case of constraints arising from measurements of the CP properties of the
SM-like Higgs boson, we distinguished how to apply these constraints. Here, we studied the
impact of applying the constraints on the CP-violating coupling of HSMτ τ̄ , either with the
public tool HiggsTools or with Eq. (5.8).

In Chapter 6, we then performed a guided parameter scan, which we dubbed Strategy 1,
for the Type II C2HDM with h2 = h125. We have shown that with this scan method, one
obtains valid parameter points that scatter around the SM-like solution. Furthermore, we
investigated the impact of the kite diagrams on the parameter space. Here, we have confirmed
that the kite diagrams are of the same order as the Barr-Zee diagrams, and therefore need to
be included in the analysis of the eEDM.

In Chapter 7, we introduced the ML algorithms we used in our second scan method, dubbed
Strategy 2. Here, we used the CMA-ES algorithm with an additional anomaly-detection
component as a novelty reward. Using these ML algorithms, we then performed an extensive
parameter scan. First, we analyzed the impact of the renormalization scheme choice for the
fermion masses. We saw that with the inclusion of the kite diagrams, one obtains qualitatively
the same results. This is in contrast to the previously obtained results in Ref. [84], where
the kite diagrams were not included in the eEDM calculation. In addition, we showed that
using ML algorithms can reveal previously overlooked valid parameter regions. Next, we
discussed the impact of including the charm quark in the eEDM calculation. Here, we saw
that the charm quark contribution to the eEDM is of order 10−29e.cm, which is larger than
the experimental limits. Therefore, including this contribution is necessary to obtain a correct
estimate of the eEDM in the C2HDM. It does not change qualitatively the phenomenology
on the CP-odd coupling cob , however. Lastly, we briefly commented on the other cases of the
C2HDM and provided an update on the possibility of sizeable CP-odd couplings in other
types of the model.



60 8. Conclusion

In summary, we performed a complete analysis of the C2HDM, using ML to explore the full
parameter space and the observables that comply with current theoretical and experimental
constraints. The ML method shown can be applied to any sampling in constrained scenarios,
such as BSM models with a large number of parameters.



Part III.

Dark Matter Analysis in the NMSSM





CHAPTER 9

Introduction

As the SM leaves open questions like the nature of DM or why there is more matter than
antimatter in the universe, we have to consider models beyond the SM. Among the many
BSM theories, supersymmetry (SUSY) answers many of the open questions. Furthermore, it
provides a relation between bosons and fermions through SUSY transformations. The scalar
sector of the Minimal Supersymmetric extension of the SM (MSSM) contains two complex
Higgs doublets, which are further extended in the NMSSM (c.f. Sec. 2.4) by a complex singlet
superfield. This introduction solves the so-called µ-problem of the MSSM, but adds additional
input parameters to the model. In SUSY, the tree-level mass of the lightest doublet-like CP-
even Higgs boson has an upper limit, such that higher-order corrections are needed in order
to comply with the measured Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV . Therefore, the mass of the Higgs
boson is now a derived parameter. This, along with the large number of input parameters,
makes parameter scans in the NMSSM difficult. Searching for benchmark scenarios that
comply with all relevant theoretical and experimental constraints is particularly difficult due
to the complexity of the parameter space.

To solve this problem, we developed NMSSMScanner [128], a framework that enables efficient
scans of the NMSSM parameter space. To obtain valid parameter points, we include all
relevant collider and low-energy constraints, as well as DM constraints. The framework is
implemented using code that computes relevant NMSSM observables and compares them
against theoretical and experimental constraints. One of these observables is the DM relic
density and the direct-detection cross section of the potential DM candidate, here, the lightest
neutralino χ̃0. To calculate these observables, we used the public code RelExt and, as part
of this project, added the NMSSM as a new model to the toolchain.

In this chapter, we provide an overview of the formulas used to calculate the DM observables.
This is followed in Ch. 10 by a brief description of the public code RelExt [129]. In Ch. 11,
we will discuss the additional observables considered in NMSSMScanner. Afterwards, we will
present our results in Ch. 12.

CHAPTER 10

RelExt - A Dark Matter Tool for Efficient Scans

Calculating DM observables such as the relic density and the direct-detection cross section
can be tedious in a BSM model like the NMSSM. Over the years, many codes like MadDM

[136–138], DarkSUSY [139], SuperISO [140] and MicrOMEGAs [66,141–145] have been developed
to calculate DM observables. However, finding the appropriate input parameter configuration
to achieve the relic abundance given in Eq. (3.22) for an arbitrary model becomes harder as
the model grows more complex. To overcome this problem, we developed the public code
RelExt, which calculates the relic density and includes a scanning tool that efficiently searches
for parameter values that yield the correct relic density. Furthermore, we have extended the
code to implement direct-detection in the NMSSM. Also, it is possible to evaluate the relic
density calculation not only at tree level but also at next-to-leading order (NLO), which we
will showcase in Part IV for the CxSM. The code can be downloaded at

https://github.com/jplotnikov99/RelExt.

RelExt is a C++ code, which calculates the relic density for DM particles that undergo the
freeze-out mechanism described in Sec. 3.5 for any model with a Z2 symmetry, which stabilizes
the DM particle. In order to run the code, the user only needs to provide a FeynRules [146]
model file. RelExt then calculates all (co-)annihilation amplitudes of the DM candidate of
the given model, generates the corresponding cross sections, and calculates with that the
thermally averaged cross section given in Eq. (9.30). The relic density is then obtained by
solving the Boltzmann equation given in Eq. (3.66). For a more detailed description of the
implementation of the C++ code, we refer to Ref. [129]. Note that in the current version of
RelExt, it is only possible to work with models that have one DM candidate. Furthermore,
BSM theories with DM annihilation processes that are CP-violating and enter the relic density
calculation, cannot be described by the derivation given in Sec. 3.5, and hence, cannot be
treated in RelExt. In this work, we provide a brief overview of the structure of the code.
Afterwards, we show how we implement the calculation of the direct-detection cross section
in RelExt.

In Figure 10.1, we show the flowchart of the code. RelExt can be divided into two parts. We
denote the first part as New Model Implementation and the second part as DM Observables

and Parameter Search. We will start our description with the former.

In this section, we briefly describe how we compute the total decay widths introduced in

CHAPTER 11

Numerical Analysis

In the previous chapters, we described in detail how the DM observables are obtained. This
chapter provides an overview of the tool NMSSMScanner, the additional observables tested,
and the computer codes used. Further, we will provide the ranges of our parameter scan.

11.1. Organization of the Scan

To perform our analysis, we use a modified version of the Python code BSMArt [161]. This
code allows us to connect all relevant programs and pass the necessary information of a given
BSM model through the program chain. In BSMArt, it is possible to use different scanning
techniques, such as Active Learning [162], Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), random
scans, or user-defined algorithms to scan the parameter space. Since BSMArt was initially
developed as a complementary framework to SARAH/SPheno [163,164], it has proven effective
across many BSM frameworks [162,165–173].

Higgs and SUSY Spectra and Decays

In order to calculate the Higgs and SUSY mass spectra, we link the Fortran code NMSSMCALC
[174] to BSMArt. The code computes the SUSY mass spectrum at leading order and evaluates
the Higgs boson mass spectrum in the CP-violating NMSSM (CNMSSM), including full one-
loop corrections [175, 176] as well as important two-loop QCD and electroweak corrections
of order O(αtαs) [177], O(α2

t ) [178] and O((αt + αλ + ακ)
2) [179]. NMSSMCALC additionally

provides predictions for the leptonic anomalous magnetic moments and the EDM at one- and
two-loop level [180, 181]. Furthermore, NMSSMCALC computes the Higgs boson decay widths
and branching ratios. These calculations have been adopted from the Fortran code HDECAY.
Also, NMSSMCALC is used to calculate the SUSY particle decays, including tree-level two-
and three-body decays, loop-induced decays, and NLO SUSY-QCD corrections for processes
involving color-charged particles [182].

Single and di-Higgs Production

In order to comply with the single Higgs boson production constraints regarding the LHC
SM-like Higgs boson data and the exclusion limits from BSM Higgs boson searches at the

then tested against the current experimental constraints. To comply with the non-resonant

SUSY Searches

In our analysis, we use the code SModelS [191–194] to check the constraints from SUSY
searches. SModelS computes the leading-order squark and gluino pair production cross section
via PYTHIA [195]. Additionally, it applies a K-Factor for the QCD corrections from NLL-

Fast [196–203] at next-to-leading logarithmic order matched to next-to-leading order. The
electroweakino pair-production cross sections are obtained using an in-house code. Here,
we apply for the NLO electroweak corrections an approximate K-factor of 1.3, which can
be used when the electroweakinos are lighter than the squarks [204, 205]. At leading order,
the mixed squark-electroweakino pair production is computed by SModelS. The total cross
section of multi-particle final states in the SUSY scenario is then obtained by combining the
production cross sections with the SUSY particle branching ratios obtained by SDECAY [206],
which includes the SUSY particle decays in the NMSSM [182] . The total cross section is
then compared with the experimental analyse.

DM Observables

As stated in the previous chapters 10 and 9, we compute the relic density and the direct-
detection cross section of the lightest neutralino using RelExt, which was extended to include
also the NMSSM as a model. The relic density is compared with the experimental limit
given in Eq. (3.22). We use Eq. (9.37) to compare with the latest exclusion bounds of the
Lux-Zeplin experiment [4].

11.3. Scan Procedure

We generate a parameter sample using the tool NMSSMScanner, optimizing an MCMC scan
with likelihood functions for each individual final state considered. This means that at first,
we perform a random scan over the ranges provided in Tab. 11.1 and use these points as
seeds for the MCMC scan. As a proof-of concept of the new tool NMSSMScanner, we try to
obtain the maximum cross section values for the resonant production of a Higgs boson X,
which subsequently decays into a SM-like plus non-SM-like Higgs boson pair X → HY , we
optimize the MCMC scan with likelihood functions L. For example 18, for the maximation
of the scalar resonance, we chose the following likelihood function

Lsmax = exp{(s0(σ × BR)/µ)} , (11.7)

where σ denotes the production cross section of HY and BR denotes the product of the
branching ratio of H and Y decaying into the considered finale state. The normalization
µ = σseed ×BRseed is calculated at the seed point. In our analysis, we set s0 = 2, as this was
found to be the optimal value for convergence.

CHAPTER 13

Conclusion

In this part of the thesis, we presented the program package NMSSMScanner, which is built to
efficiently scan the complex parameter space of the NMSSM. Within the scope of this project,
we implemented the NMSSM relic density and the direct-detection cross section calculation in
the public code RelExt. We have presented the necessary framework for calculating the relic
density and the direct-detection cross section in the NMSSM. Afterward, we gave an overview
of the public code RelExt in Ch. 10 and described how we automate the implementation
of an arbitrary model in RelExt. In Ch. 11, we presented how we organize the program
chain in the program package NMSSMScanner. Here, we discuss the various experimental
constraints included in our analysis. In Chapter 12, we presented as a proof of concept
benchmark points, which maximize the cross section of a SM-like and non-SM-like Higgs
boson pair, which is produced by a resonant scalar or pseudoscalar Higgs boson, in various
decay channels. Further, we extended the investigation compared to Ref. [128] by providing,
for each benchmark point, information on the DM observables, i.e., the DM relic density and
the direct-detection cross section. Also, we investigated the possibility of obtaining the correct
relic density in the NMSSM while still complying with the exclusion limit of LUX-Zeplin.
We have shown that there is still a parameter region that saturates the relic density, complies
with the exclusion limits of the Lux-Zeplin collaboration, and lies above the neutrino floor.
In summary, we provided a proof of concept for our new package NMSSMScanner and the
extension of RelExt, which can serve as a starting point for future investigations of the
allowed parameter space and DM observables of the NMSSM.

CHAPTER 14

Introduction

The SM has unsolved problems, one of which is the nature of dark matter. As described
in Ch. 3, it is possible to extract from the CMB the current energy budget of dark matter
in the universe. The dark matter relic abundance has been measured by the PLANCK
collaboration to be Ωch

2 = 0.1200 ± 0.0012 [3]. This value acts as a constraining factor on
the parameter space of models with dark matter candidates. Calculating the relic abundance
from a theoretical point of view, for any model, involves computing the (co-)annihilation
cross sections of dark matter into SM particles. In practice, this calculation is generally
done at leading-order. However, as experiments become more and more precise, theoretical
predictions also need to be precise. In Refs. [226–229], the electroweak next-to-leading order
effects on the relic density have been investigated in the framework of the inert-doublet
2HDM. In this work we computed the full electroweak and QCD higher-order effects in the
framework of the CxSM, described in Sec. 2.2. As described in Ch. 10, it is possible to
choose between a variety of codes to calculate the relic abundance at leading-order for an
arbitrary model. However, at next-to-leading order, this calculation becomes more difficult.
In MicrOMEGAs [141,142,144,145] it is possible to include next-to-leading order corrections via
predefined functions. Furthermore, the code DM@NLO [230] provides the next-to-leading order
(SUSY) QCD corrections for dark matter (co-)annihilation in the Minimal Supersymmetric
Standard Model. In this work, we use our code RelExt, which we introduced in Ch. 10,
and extended the already implemented relic density at leading-order in the context of the
CxSM by the calculation of next-to-leading order electroweak and QCD corrections to the
annihilation cross section of a dark matter pair into SM particles. This work will serve as
an initial example of the implementation of next-to-leading order corrections in RelExt for
a specific model, as the goal is to later extend the code in such a way to allow for an easy
implementation of next-to-leading order corrections in RelExt for arbitrary models.

We will present this work as follows. We outline the general idea of the next-to-leading order
calculation in Sec. 14.1. As ultraviolet and infrared divergences can arise at next-to-leading
order calculations, we have to cure these with an appropriate regularisation and renormal-
ization scheme. We provide an overview of the used renormalization schemes in the CxSM
and describe how we treat infrared divergences in our processes in Ch. 15. Furthermore, we
present the in Ch. 16 the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and also the scan
ranges of our example parameter sample. In Ch. 17, we show our obtained results.

Renormalization and the Treatment of Infrared Divergences in the CxSM

In higher-order calculations, ultraviolet (UV) and infrared (IR) divergences may arise. These
must be handled appropriately to obtain physically meaningful and interpretable results.
Ultraviolet divergences are handled by regularization and renormalization schemes. To cure
the IR divergences, a different approach is used; see Sec. 15.5.

Dimensional regularization is a commonly used regularization method. In this approach, the
loop integrals appearing in the calculation are evaluated in D = 4 − 2ϵ dimensions. The
divergences then manifest as poles of inverse powers of ϵ (ϵ−1 for UV divergences and ϵ−1 and
ϵ−2 for IR divergences). To render the physical amplitudes for a calculated process free of
the UV poles, the input parameters must be redefined. The renormalized parameter κ and
the corresponding counterterm δκ are introduced such that the bare parameter κ0, which
emerges in the unrenormalized Lagrangian L0, is defined as

κ0 = κ+ δκ . (15.1)

Furthermore, the bare fields ψ0 are defined by a shift of the wave-function renormalization
constant Zψ such that

As we consider in the calculation of the relic density final states with electric and color charge,
photons, and gluons appear in the loop diagrams. These types of diagrams lead to infrared
divergences. According to the Kinoshita-Lee-Nauenberg theorem, IR safety is guaranteed
upon including real corrections [252, 253]. The total UV- and IR-convergent cross section is
then given by

While the Eq. (15.50) is infrared finite, the virtual and real emission cross sections are sepa-

gauge bosons, such as photons or gluons, in loop diagrams. In particular, they enter through
the IR-divergent derivatives of the self-energies, which are used in the wave function renor-

massless particle in the loop. In the case of the real corrections, the IR divergences stem
from the divergent phase space of the emitted massless gauge boson in the soft limit, where
the momentum of the emitted particle becomes very small. To obtain a Lorentz-invariant
cancellation of the IR divergences, dimensional regularization should be applied, such that
the integration over phase space must be performed in D = 4−2ϵ dimensions. However, since
it very difficult to analytically extract the IR poles from the 2 → 3 phase-space integral to
cancel them with the corresponding IR poles from the virtual corrections, this method is not
suitable for numerical applications. Hence, we will use the Catani-Seymour dipole subtraction
method [254], which we will discuss in Sec. 15.5.2. In order to use this method, we need to
calculate the real corrections in the full three-body phase space dΠ3. For this purpose, we
will give a brief overview of the derivation of the three-body phase space.

16.2. Experimental Constraints

Electroweak Precision Parameters

Due to the additional scalar particle in the CxSM, additional contributions appear in the
self-energies of the gauge bosons. These lead to deviations from the SM predictions. These
deviations can be parametrized by the oblique parameters S, T , and U [97]. We check via
ScannerS, which uses a fit result, the compatibility of the theoretical and experimental values.

Higgs Searches

The measurements at the LHC of the discovered Higgs boson as well as the searches for
additional scalar particles constrain the parameter space of the CxSM. In order to obtain
valid parameter points, ScannerS is linked to the public code HiggsTools [109], which is a
unification of the modules HiggsSignals [112] and HiggsBounds [260]. Here, we check the
agreement of the signal rates of the SM-like Higgs boson with the experimental data at the 2σ
level by HiggsSignals. The constraints from the searches for the additional scalar particles
in theory are included by HiggsBounds.

Dark Matter Observables

We impose that the parameter points must fulfill at leading-order the relic density constraint
by the PLANCK experiment given in Eq. (3.22). This is checked with our code RelExt [129].
In the CxSM, the direct detection constraint does not affect the parameter space, as the LO
cross section is suppressed by the small DM velocity and therefore negligible.

CHAPTER 18

Conclusion

In this part of the thesis, we investigated the impact of the relic density in the framework of
the CxSM, which we introduced in Sec. 2.2. Within the scope of this project, we extended the
public code RelExt with the calculation of the relic density at next-to-leading order, which
we will extend in future work to automate the implementation of higher-order calculations in
an arbitrary model.

We have presented how the relic density is obtained at next-to-leading order. In Ch. 15, we
demonstrated how we obtain UV- and IR-finite cross sections for our calculation. Afterwards,
we presented the applied theoretical and experimental constraints and the scan ranges of our
parameter sample. Finally, in Ch. 17, we presented the impact of the higher-order corrections
on the dark matter relic abundance. Here, we provided as a proof-of-concept the results
first only with next-to-leading order QCD corrections. Next, we presented the electroweak
and the QCD corrections and the impact of different renormalization schemes. We have
shown that the higher-order corrections can lead to either an increase or a decrease of the
relic density. This has an important phenomenological consequence: higher-order corrections
can invalidate previously valid parameter points by increasing the relic density such that it
exceeds the observed dark matter relic abundance measured by the PLANCK experiment
[3]. Vice versa, due to possibly negative higher-order corrections to the relic density, it can
occur, that previously discarded parameter points, which oversaturated the relic density, can
become valid again. Furthermore, we have shown that the theoretical uncertainty between the
renormalization schemes are small if the variation of the input parameters that are affected
by the change in scheme is small.

Overall, we have shown that the inclusion of higher-order calculations are important to explore
the parameter space of a given dark matter model.





Part V.

Conclusion and Overview





CHAPTER 19

Final Conclusion and Outlook

The success story of the Standard Model of particle physics was further advanced by the
discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012. However, despite its many precise predictions, the
Standard Model still lacks solutions to some unanswered problems. In this thesis, we focused
on understanding the nature of dark matter in the universe by investigating various theories
beyond the Standard Model. A very important observable is the dark matter relic density
Ωch

2, which has been measured by the PLANCK collaboration to be

Ωch
2 = 0.1200± 0.0012 . (19.1)

The computation of the relic density in a theory beyond the Standard Model can become
tedious, in particular for more complex models. This task becomes even more difficult when
the goal is to find the parameter configuration that yields the correct experimental relic
density. To solve this issue, we developed, within the scope of this thesis, the C++ code
RelExt, which automates the computation of the relic density via freeze-out for an arbitrary
model with a dark matter candidate stabilized by a discrete symmetry. Furthermore, we
implemented search algorithms that conveniently provide the parameter configurations which
yield the experimentally observed relic density. Also, due to its modular structure, the code
can easily be extended to implement new features, such as computing the direct-detection
cross section or calculating higher-order corrections to the relic density.

In Part I, we briefly introduced the Standard Model, and the beyond-the-Standard Model
(BSM) theories investigated in this thesis, which are the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model, the Complex Two-Higgs Doublet Model, and the Next-To Minimal Super-
symmetric Standard Model. Afterward, we gave a brief introduction to the Standard Model of
Cosmology. Furthermore, we provided derivations of the Boltzmann equation for calculating
the dark matter relic density and of the direct detection cross section.

To provide precise theoretical predictions, we need a deeper understanding of the experimen-
tal constraints and their interplay within BSM theories. Therefore, in Part II of this thesis,
we studied the interplay of collider and electric dipole constraints by investigating the al-
lowed CP-violation of the coupling between a fermion pair and a Standard Model-like Higgs
boson. We first introduced expressions for calculating the electric dipole moment, including
kite diagrams, which were not included in previous works, followed by a description of the



134 19. Final Conclusion and Outlook

theoretical and experimental constraints used in our parameter scan. In Ch. 6, we presented
the results using traditional scan methods, i.e., using a guided scan method. To potentially
reveal previously overlooked regions in the parameter space, we employed machine learning
algorithms, specifically the CMA-ES algorithm, to explore it. In Ch. 7, we provided a short
description of the machine learning algorithm, as well as the presentation of our results.

Exploring the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model is
a complicated and computationally intensive task. To circumvent this issue, we presented
in Part III our new tool NMSSMScanner, which provides a convenient way to explore the
parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. In Ch. 9, we
presented the theoretical framework necessary for the evaluation of the relic density and
the direct detection cross section in this model. Within the scope of this work, RelExt,
introduced in Ch. 10, was extended to include the calculation of these dark matter observables.
Afterward, we provided an overview of the tool NMSSMScanner, presenting the experimental
and theoretical constraints, as well as the computer codes used in the program chain. As a
proof-of-concept of this tool, we maximized the production cross section of a resonant non-
Standard Model Higgs boson into various final states, as well as investigating the dark matter
observables in the Next-to Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model. A detailed description
of our results is given in Ch. 12.

In the final Part IV of this thesis, we computed the dark matter relic abundance at next-to-
leading order electroweak and QCD in the framework of the Complex Singlet Extension of the
Standard Model. In order to do so, we implemented the next-to-leading order annihilation
amplitudes squared in RelExt. In Ch. 15, we presented the prescriptions needed in order to
obtain UV- and IR-finite annihilation cross sections. Afterward, we presented the applied
theoretical and experimental constraints, as well as the scan ranges used in the investigated
parameter sample. In Ch. 17, we showed the impact of higher-order corrections on the
relic density, as well as the phenomenological consequences of these, where we saw that the
higher-order corrections can both increase or decrease the computed relic density, making
the higher-order calculation an important contribution to future studies of the validity of
parameter points.

Even though the Standard Model is a success story in itself, the unanswered questions show
us that there is still new physics to be discovered. In order to do so, we need precise cal-
culations within the Standard Model as well as in theories beyond the Standard Model. In
particular, there is a lack of precision in calculations in dark matter models. However, exper-
iments for dark matter searches become increasingly precise. Therefore, the need for precise
theoretical predictions becomes increasingly relevant to solving the mystery of dark matter in
the universe. With this thesis, we provided a contribution to further proceed on this path.

APPENDIX B

RelExt - Overview on the Mathematica Code and Direct Detection Class

B.1. Mathematica Code

In this section, we provide a more detailed description of the Mathematica code implemented
in RelExt. Here, we will follow the description in Ref. [129].

The implementation of a new model in RelExt is fully automated. Here, the implementation
involves two Mathematica scripts, which are saved in the directory mathematica. The first
script FR_to_CH_FA.m automatically converts the FeynRules model file into FeynArts (FA)
and CalcHep (CH) files. The generated files can then be found in the folders FA_modfiles and
CH_modfiles. These folders are localized in the $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/FR_modfiles/

directory.26 The second Mathematica script, amp2cpp.m, generates and stores all amplitudes
needed to compute the Freeze-Out relic abundance for a DM particle, as well as all information
required to implement a new model. This script can be divided into three different building
blocks: the amplitude generation block, the decay width generation block and the conversion
from Mathematica to C++ code block. In the following, we provide an overview of the most
important functions, lists, and segments for each block.

The most important elements of the amplitude generation block are

• particlelist is a list, where the FA particle identifiers, their masses, the names and
PDG numbers are stored. Here, we also include anti-particles; however, exclude Gold-
stone bosons and ghost particles.

• The function determineDof[pID_] determines the degrees of freedom of the particle,
which is given by the FA identifier pID_.

• The lists dslist(FA particle identifier), dsmass(mass), dsnames(name) and dsDof(degrees
of freedom) store the information of the dark sector particles. The corresponding infor-
mation are given in the brackets.

26
$RelExt denotes the path, where RelExt is installed, and ModelName is a placeholder name for the name of
the user‘s model.



138 B RelExt - Overview on the Mathematica Code and Direct Detection Class

• alldiags provides all tree-level 2 → 2 Feynman diagrams, with two dark sector parti-
cles in the initial states and none in the final state.

• The function removeDuplicate[] is used to remove redundant processes from the di-
agsgrouped list. Here, a new list listofprocs is generated, which is the final list
containing all processes necessary for computing the relic abundance. This includes all
channels with two dark sector particles in the initial state and none in the final state.
In the case of co-annihilation, this leads to redundancy, as channels with the same final
state but with an initial state where the particles are swapped also contribute to the
relic density. The amplitude, however, is analytically the same. Therefore, we compute
only one amplitude, and remove the other one from the list listofprocs. The same
reasoning applies to processes whose initial state is the charge conjugate of a previous
one. To still obtain the correct relic density, we apply a multiplicative factor to the
Boltzmann equation to compensate for the removed channels.

• In order to identify all couplings or coupling combinations in the amplitudes, we imple-
mented the function breakdownAmp[process_,amp_], where the input parameters are
a list element process_ of the list listofprocs and the amplitude amp_. To reduce
computation time in the relic density calculation, these expressions are stored as tokens.

• In order to compute the amplitudes for each process in listofprocs, we implemented
the function calcAmps[] in our script. The generated amplitudes are stored in the
list ampslist and the relevant Freeze-Out processes in the list foutlist. We use the
lists coefficientlist,mandellist, and tokens in this routine to tokenize the squared
amplitude. Further, we save the masses of the participating particles in the lists mi, mj,
mk and ml.

• We identify the s-channel contributions in the amplitudes with the function checkden-

pol[amp_], where the input is a list element of mandellist. If a s-channel is found, we
transform the denominator of the respective amplitude as described in Sec. 10.1, with
the function addwidthsub[den_], where the input is the denominator of the amplitude
amp_ as a string.

• The masses and the total decay widths of the s-channel mediators are stored in the list
relevantWs.

• For each list element in foutlist, the amplitudes squared are generated with the func-
tioncalcAmp2s[]. Each expression is stored in the list final. Note, that the compila-
tion of this function can take several minutes, depending on the number of list elements
in foutlist.

The second block is the width generation block. This block is similar to the previous block,
with one main difference. If the found mediator particle is a scalar or pseudoscalar, we do
not calculate the total width of this particle with FeynCalc, but instead with the procedure
provided in Sec. 10.1. The functions and lists used in this block are

• The FA particle identifiers and the decay widths of the s-channel mediators are stored
in the lists relevantWsfield and relevantWidth, respectively. Note that the total
decay width of the SM gauge bosons is taken from the input model files.



B.1. Mathematica Code 139

• All relevant decay processes for the computation of the total width are stored in fout-

listDecays. Here, we save the FA particle identifier in each column, with the first
column denoting the decaying particle and the other two the final-state particles.

• We identify the type of the participating particles in the decay with the function de-

terminType[sts_,ind_]. The inputs are any row of the list foutDecayslist sts_

and the corresponding column number int_.

• The generated squared amplitudes for the decays and their decay widths are stored in
the lists finalDecays and finalDecaysWidth, respectively.

The last block is the Mathematica to C++ conversion part. Here, the previously obtained
expressions for the (co-)annihilation amplitudes squared, the partial decay widths and the
relevant informations of the models are converted into C++ files. This block consists of the
following functions and lists

• The list inifunc[i] is used to store for each unique channel that contributes to the
computation of the relic abundance, the processname, the mass, the FA identifier, and
the tokenized amplitudes squared. The input parameter i is an integer and goes from
1 to the total number of different initial states.

• external and internal are lists that store all external and internal variables of the
model and their definitions, respectively.

• The list neutraldsmasses stores all the masses of the neutral dark sector particles.

• processnameDecays and possibleiniDecays are auxiliary lists that store the names
of the decay processes and the corresponding decaying particles, respectively.

• inifuncDecays[i] is analogous to inifunc[i] but is used for decay processes. In addi-
tion, it contains two extra columns corresponding to the couplings and particleType

lists.

• runMasses contains the masses of the strange, charm, bottom, and top quarks.

• model.hpp, model.cpp, init.cpp, parametermap.cpp, loadparameters.cpp, and load-
tokens.cpp contain the declarations and initialization routines for all external and in-
ternal model parameters, tokens, amplitudes squared, partial and total decay widths,
dark-sector masses, and the masses and widths of the relevant s-channel propagators.
The file model.hpp is located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/, while all remaining files
are stored in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/. If external parameters depend on
the running quark masses contained in runMasses, they must be redefined in loadpa-

rameters.cpp such that their values are updated whenever the renormalization scale
of the running masses changes. The only exception is the top quark, for which the
user-defined pole mass is used.

• calcwidths.cpp contains the routines for computing the running quark masses at a
given energy scale as well as the total widths of the relevant s-channel mediators. For
decay processes, the running masses are evaluated at a scale equal to the pole mass of
the decaying particle, whereas for DM (co-)annihilation processes, the scale is chosen
as twice the DM mass.

• all[possibleini].cpp contains the expressions for the amplitudes squared of all DM
(co-)annihilation channels associated with a given initial state [possibleini]. These
files are located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s, with separate files for
different initial states.



140 B RelExt - Overview on the Mathematica Code and Direct Detection Class

• [possibleini]flux.cpp contains the amplitudes squared multiplied by the correspond-
ing flux factors, where the latter are defined in $RelExt/sources/utils.cpp. An
additional multiplicative factor, symfac, may be included to account for equivalent pro-
cesses removed by the removeDuplicate[] routine. These files are stored in $RelEx-

t/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s.

• totalW[possibleini]Decays.cpp contains the expressions for the partial decay widths
of the relevant s-channel mediators, where [possibleini]Decays denotes the decaying
particle. The files are located in $RelExt/md_[ModelName]/sources/amp2s, with one
file per mediator. For scalar and pseudoscalar particles, hard-coded partial_width

functions are employed. These functions take as input the particle types in the final
state, their masses, and the couplings extracted from the amplitudes squared, as de-
scribed in Sec. 10.1. For all other particle types, the decay widths are computed using
FeynCalc. Off-shell decay channels are assigned a width of zero.

• prtcls.cpp contains the definitions of all particle and anti-particle names used in the
model. Particles that are their own anti-particles are listed only once.

Abstract

In this work, we review 3-dimensional gravity by canonically analyzing the Hilbert-

Palatini action. We apply a time gauge used in 4-dimensional loop quantum grav-

ity [14] to the simpler case of the 3-dimensional loop quantum gravity. By time

gauge fixing this Hilbert-Palatini action it leads to the Gauss constraints, the spa-

tial diffeomorphism constraints, the Hamiltonian constraint and a new constraint

C. The gauge symmetries generated by this new constraints are spacetime diffeo-

morphism and SO(2) gauge transformations. We solve the dynamics of the theory

by providing a regularization of the generalized projector operator in terms of the

Hamiltonian constraint. We provide the definition of the physical scalar product

which can be represented in terms of a sum over finite spinfoam amplitudes. Then

we establish a clear-cut link between the canonical quantization of the new theory

to the spinfoam model (Ponzano-Regge model) defined in terms of the SU(2) spin

networks.

Chapter 1

Introduction and Motivation

1.1 Quantum Gravity

The task of quantizing gravity is one of the outstanding problems of modern

theoretical physics. Attempts to reconcile quantum theory and general relativity

(GR) date back to the early part of the twentieth century. Several decades of

hard work have yielded an abundance of insights into quantum field theory. But

despite this enormous effort, no one has yet succeeded in formulating a complete,

self-consistent quantum theory of gravity [5].

Einstein’s description of gravity as a curvature of spacetime (geometry of curved

spacetime) was seen as a game changer at the time, as this idea totally moved away

from the notion of gravity as a force. The consequence of this was the formulation

of the theory of GR which gave a deep insight into the geometric structure of the

universe at the macroscopic level.

Quantum mechanics (QM), which describes the microscopic world was formulated

based on the laws of probability. It allows for a discrete energy spectrum instead of

a continuous radiation. QM uses the time evolution of quantum states described by

the Schrodinger equation in which the Hamiltonian generates the time evolution.

This means that physical quantities can change only in discrete amounts and not

in a continuous way [27].

Our understanding of physics, and in general nature have been greatly influenced

by QM and GR. Both principles have revolutionized the pivotal structures of New-

tonian physics. The notion of absolute time and space ceases to exist, but rather

space and time and distances between points of the spacetime manifold, that is,

the metric themselves become dynamical objects [27, 28]. Further, the determin-

istic nature of Newton’s equations of motion evaporates at a fundamental level,

1

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



rather dynamics is reigned by probabilities underlying the Heisenberg uncertainty

principle.

A usual phenomenon in fundamental physics is to reconcile two different concep-

tual theories to find a new synthesis, a satisfactory physical theory must therefore

combine both of these fundamental principles, QM and GR, in a consistent way

and which will be called quantum gravity (QG). However, despite the success sto-

ries of both QM and GR, the quantization of the gravitational field has turned

out to be one of the most challenging unsolved problems in theoretical and math-

ematical physics.

The reason for this incompatibility is that, GR requires spacetime to be a dy-

namical field, describing the notion of force as a geometry and also requires an

independent background structure. On the other hand, QM requires a dynamical

field to be quantized, and in addition requires a non-dynamical background space-

time (Hilbert space) for it to take place. In GR, spacetime is dynamical, while

in QM, any dynamical entity is made up of quanta and can be in probabilistic

superposition states.

Not only are there conceptual differences in quantizing gravity, there are techni-

cal obstacles also facing the new synthesis. Einstein’s equations which governs

the theory of gravity are highly non-linear, and hence very difficult to solve. In

addition, conventional field quantization methods which are based on the weak-

field perturbation expansion fail in their application to GR since they yield a

non-renormalizable theory. GR, hence must be replaced by a more fundamental

description that appropriately includes the quantum degrees of freedom of gravity

[24].

However, it is clear that while GR has given a very consistent framework for doing

classical physics, it has not yet been successful in bringing the quantum realm

in its wake [21]. Attempts have been made for decades to formulate a consistent

theory of quantum gravity, but with no success so far.

1.2 Loop Quantum Gravity

The past decades have seen an increase in active research in the field of quantum

theory of gravity, with some claiming to have found a quantum theory of gravity.

Notably among them is string theory, which is based on the physical hypothesis

that elementary objects are extended rather than particle-like [27]. A very rich

unified theory which includes Yang-Mills fields and gravitons, and free of ultravio-

let divergences are a few of string theory’s successful story. However, this comes at

2

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



a cost of additional physics such as supersymmetry, extra dimensions, an infinite

number of fields with an arbitrary masses and spins.

In light of this another active area of research in QG is Loop Quantum Gravity

(LQG) which takes a different approach to string theory. LQG is a canonical

and background independent base approach to the quantization of gravity paying

special attention to the conceptual lessons of GR [9, 23, 27, 28]. It proposes that

spacetime is actually divided into small chucks, when you zoom out it appears

to be a smooth sheet, but when you zoom in, it is a bunch of dots connected by

lines or loops. These small fibres, which are woven together offer an explanation

of gravity.

LQG is based on a Hamiltonian formulation of GR at the classical level. In this

formulation, spacetime is foliated into a family of hypersurfaces of constant time

with coordinates on each slice. LQG is a straightforward quantization procedure

of GR with the physical inputs of the theory been the well-tested physical theories

of QM and GR, there are no major additional physical hypothesis or assumption

made in the construction of the theory [27]. All it tries to do is to merge the

conceptual ideas of GR into QM. In addition, LQG is based on assumption that

even if Einstein’s equations are modified at high energy, the general-relativistic

notion of space and time are assumed to be true.

The theory is formulated in the more physical four dimensional case. It was

initially formulated in terms of the metric variables which was due to Arnowitt,

Deser and Misner [28], hence the name ADM formulation. In this formulation, the

canonical variables are the metric tensor of three dimensional spatial slices qab(x, t)

(here a, b are 3d space indices) and it’s conjugate momentum πab [23, 28] following

an ADM decomposition of the action. The decomposition results in the spatial

diffeomorphism V (qab, π
ab) and Hamiltonian constraints S(qab, π

ab), however the

non-linear dependence on the canonical variables especially by the Hamiltonian

constraint makes it mathematically difficult to promote the constraints into quan-

tum operators.

To address the problem of promoting the constraints into operators, a tetrad

formulation was introduced. The tetrad is defined as eI = eIµdx
µ such that gµν =

In this new formulation, additional degrees of freedom are introduced due to the

redundancy exhibited by the new variables: this occurs as there are nine Ea
i

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



to describe the six components of qab. As a result an additional constraints-

Gauss constraint- in terms of the new variables makes this redundancy manifest.

However, the problems similar to using the ADM formulation arise when one tries

In the pursuit of solving the non-polynomial associated with the Hamiltonian

constraint, Ashtekar introduced a new configuration variable (Aia) that behaves

as a complex SU(2) connection. The three constraints now become polynomials

in the Ashtekar variables i.e the Ashtekar connection Aia and the densitized triad

Ea
i . This simplification open up ways to quantize the constraint.

However, despite this simplification there are still some issues in properly defining

the constraints and solving them. This comes from the fact that the Ashtekar

connection is defined as a complex variable, hence in the quantization of the theory

it is difficult to ensure one recovers real GR as opposed to complex GR, unless

the reality condition is imposed [27]. In addition, there are difficulties of a rather

technical nature related to the complete characterization of dynamics and the

quantization of the Hamiltonian constraint [23].

Despite these challenges, LQG has been able to predict the discreteness of geo-

metrical operators such as area and volume. This discreteness becomes important

at the Planck scale while the geometric operators crowds very rapidly at low en-

ergy scale. This property of the geometric operators is consistent with the smooth

spacetime picture of classical GR [23].

In carrying out canonical quantization, the guiding principle is mostly that of

Dirac. The first is to find a representation of the phase space variables as operators,

acting on some kinematical Hilbert space Hkin. This representation of the phase

space variables should map Poisson brackets into commutators. Next is to define

the constraints into self-adjoint operators in Hkin, and finally the solutions of

these constraints are characterize to define an inner product leading to a physical

Hilbert space Hphy.

The Poisson bracket between the Ashtekar-Barbero connection and the densitized

triad resulted in a delta function (distribution), this leads to a not well-defined

function. A regularization of the Poisson bracket is needed to address this problem,

and this is done by smearing the phase space variables to obtain the holonomy-flux

algebra. The regularization open up ways to quantize these constraints, and such

they (constraints) become operators on a kinematical Hilbert space. For more

on loop quantum gravity the reader is advice to read [23, 27, 28] and references

therein.

4

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



1.3 Loops and Spin Networks

The choice of different algebra of basic field functions to promote to quantum

operators makes LQG stands out among other different quantization techniques.

That choice is a non-canonical algebra based on the holonomies of the gravitational

connection [23, 27].

The holonomy in LQG becomes a quantum operator creating ”loop states”1. In a

background independent theory like LQG, the position of a loop state is relevant

only with respect to other loops, and not with respect to the background [27].

The space spanned by these loop states are not too singular nor too many, thereby

providing a basis for the Hilbert space of LQG. A finite linear combination of some

of these loop states form a well defined orthonormal basis in the Hilbert space of

a lattice Yang-Mills theory. These orthonormal basis are the spin networks states

which eventually form the basis of the mathematical structure of LQG.

As stated earlier, one will like to know what the quanta of space (quantum prop-

erties of space) are, and how to describe them, in the pursuit of a quantum theory

of spacetime. Interactions of physical systems with other systems may occur in

”quanta” and these quanta are determined by the spectral properties of the op-

erators representing the quantities involved in the interaction with the systems.

The interactions with the gravitational field (spacetime) are through geometric

structures of the physical space resulting in measurements of length, area and

volume.

The spectrum of both volume and area turns out to be discrete. From the spectral

of the volume, the quanta of space can be thought of as grains of space. These

grains of space lie adjacent to each, where in this case adjacency means being

contiguous, or being in touch, or being nearby. If one consider a quantum state

of space formed by P grains of space, where some are in contact with one another

[27].

Then representing this state as an abstract graph Γ with P nodes: these nodes of

the graph represent the grains of the space; the links of the graph connect adjacent

grains and represent the surfaces separating two adjacent grains. The quantum

state is then characterized by the graph Γ, with the labels on the nodes and on

the links, and a graph with these labels is called a spin network.

LQG has been able to predict the discretness of the spectrum of geometrical op-

erators like area and volume. The formulation of LQG in terms of the Ashtekar-

1In the loop representation formulation of Maxwell theory, a loop state is a state in which
the electric field vanishes everywhere except along a single Faraday line

5

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



Barbero variables result in the Gauss constraints, the spatial diffeomorphism con-

straints and the Hamiltonian constraint. Defining cylindrical functional as quan-

tum states of the Ashtekar connection, spin network states establish themselves

as solutions to both Gauss and spatial diffeomorphism constraints. Unfortunately,

this can’t be said about the Hamiltonian constraint.

1.4 Motivation and Goal of Thesis

General relativity in three dimensions is said to be ”simple” but not trivial mak-

ing it an interesting, and as such a large area of research providing an insight

into quantum gravity for the more physical four dimension. Physically three di-

mensional gravity is a topological field theory, meaning it has no degrees of [5]

freedom2 and its manifold is regarded as a two surface with time.

Conceptually both (2 + 1)-dimensional gravity and (3 + 1)-dimensional gravity

are equivalent and many of the fundamental issues carry over to quantum gravity

at the lower dimensional setting. Although (2+1)-dimensional model is much

simpler, mathematically and physically, and we can write down a quantum theory

for the model.

There are however few instances were (2+1)-dimensional solutions are quite dif-

ferent physically from those of (3+1)-dimensional, and in addition the (2+1)-

dimensional model does not help in understanding the dynamics of quantum grav-

ity. Based on the analysis of conceptual problems such as nature of time, the role

of topology and topology change, the relationship among different approaches to

quantization, the model has really proven highly instructive [5].

Canonical analysis of (2+1)-dimensional gravity [3] result in the flatness and Gauss

constraints, defining a normal to the hypersurface x0 =const, the Hamiltonian and

spatial diffeomorphism constraints are derived. These constraints generate equal

time hypersurface which can be deformed and pushed forward in various ways. A

geometric algebra reflected in the Poisson algebra of the constraints- known as the

Dirac’s hypersurface deformation algebra3 is satisfied by these deformations of the

hypersurface. However a quantum representation of this algebra (see [3] and other

references therein for more details) has not been reached yet even in the simple

case of three dimensional gravity.

2There are no gravitational waves in the classical theory, and no propagating gravitons in the
quantum theory.

3The Dirac algebra is universal, i.e. it is the same algebra for any theory of hypersurfaces
embedded in a higher dimensional manifold.

6

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



In the 4d decomposition of spacetime, the Ashtekar connection transforms under

the local SU(2) or SO(3) transformation with the action being Lorentz invariant.

Since three dimensional gravity is simple, one will like to explore if it is possible

to time gauge just like in four dimensional gravity, and if successful what can we

learn from it with respect to the 4d case. Symmetry plays a crucial role in any

gauge theory, and as such performing a time gauge fixing in three dimensional

gravity, one expect a break in the original symmetry of the theory.

Description of a quantum space is an issue in quantum gravity, in (3+1)-dimensional

LQG and as well in (2 + 1)-dimensional LQG. The quantum space in both cases

are describe in terms of SU(2) spin networks, the question then is, if the 2+1 time

gauge fixing of the Palatini action is invariant under SO(2), then can we define

a quantum space of this theory in terms of spin networks invariant under SO(2)

transformation.

Addressing some of the questions raised above, and also understanding the physics

that can be studied as a result of the time gauge fixing in (2+1)-dimensional LQG.

In addition, how does the time gauge contribute meaningfully in understanding

loop quantum gravity, in general motivated this research.

1.5 Organization of Work

We have tried to make this work self-contained and to present all materials needed

for understanding the foundations and the theoretical framework of loop quantum

gravity and in particular the notion of time gauge fixing in (2 + 1)-dimensional

loop quantum gravity. Furthermore, we have tried to understand the dynamics of

the time gauge action in canonical quantization.

In chapter 2 we discuss the canonical formulation of 3d gravity. We begin with a

review on the main ideas of the general theory on canonical formalism. We then

discuss the canonical analysis of three dimensional Hilbert-Palatini action as a

example of the canonical formalism. A time gauge is introduced and a canonical

analysis of the Hilbert-Palatini action is carried out in terms of the time gauge.

Subsequent discussions on the time evolution and algebra of constraints are carried

out.

In chapter 3 we discuss the classical representation of the phase space variables.

To this the holonomies and the flux are introduced which are seen as the basic set

phase space function for quantization. Then the Poisson bracket between these

phase space variables are computed to give a much simpler expression (algebra)

thereby making quantization of these variables feasible.

7

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



Chapter 4 looks at the kinematical Hilbert space needed for quantization of our

theory. Cylindrical functions as basic observables for quantization are discussed, in

addition an inner product of these cylindrical functions are defined leading to the

Cauchy completion of the space of the cylindrical functions. Then orthonormal

basis of the kinematical Hilbert space are introduced leading to an SO(2) spin

networks.

In chapter 5 we discuss the dynamics of the theory in terms of spin foam rep-

resentation. We begin by introducing a projector operator and then define a

regularization of the projector operator. Then the matrix element of this pro-

jector operator is constructed. This matrix element is seen as the start of the

quantization procedure. Finally, a spin foam representation of the matrix element

is carried out.

In chapter 6 a summary of the results of the work is given.

1.6 Conventions and Notations

clidean space as hyperplanes in four-dimensional Euclidean space [5]) parametrized

by a gauge connection and it’s conjugate momentum, as has been shown in the

(3 + 1)-dimensional situation [14].

This chapter is devoted to the canonical formulation of gravity, in particular,

Einstein’s theory of gravity in three dimensions (two space, one time). We shall

A description of a three dimensional gravity’s phase space will be looked at.

2.1 General Theory on Canonical Formalism

A dynamical system in classical mechanics consists of a phase space1Γ which is

a Poisson (usually symplectic) manifold and a function Hcl : Γ −→ R called

the (classical) Hamiltonian of energy function. For example, for a single particle

moving along a real line, Γ is the cotangent bundle T (R)∗.

In quantum machanics, the phase space Γ is replaced by the set of rays in a

complex Hilbert space H, and the space F(Γ) of functions on Γ by the algebra

Op(H) of (not necessarily bounded) operators on H. For example, in the case of

a single particle moving along the real line, H is the space of square-integrable

functions of x ∈ R.

In section 1.4, three dimensional gravity was discussed as a topological theory

with no local degrees of freedom. This feature makes the description of spacetime

as a collection of patches (contractible open set of spacetime manifold), solutions

of the Einstein equations are isometric to a model spacetime which is determined

by the signature and the sign (or vanishing) of the cosmological constant.

For example, in Lorentzian signature with vanishing cosmological constant, the

model spacetime is Minkowski space while in the Euclidean signature and positive

cosmological constant it is the three-sphere, and so on [5]. This picture leads to

the description of (2 + 1)-dimensional gravity in terms of “geometric structures.”

Depending on the topology of the manifoldM, these local solutions may be glued

together to obtain non-trivial global solutions of the Einstein equations. This

is mathematically executed by the isometry group of the local model spacetime

(the 3d Poincare group ISO(2, 1) or the orthogonal group SO(4) in the examples

mentioned above). These groups are the local isometries of the model spacetime.

Matter in the form of point particles can be described geometrically in terms

of defects of the model spacetime. The space of all these geometric structures,

suitably defined, constitutes the phase space of 3d gravity. In addition, the phase

space provides us with a symplectic form (Poisson brackets) which is needed for

canonical quantization.

Canonical formulation plays a big role in the quantization of gravity. In chapter 1,

we discussed about quantum gravity precisely loop quantum gravity and the chal-

lenges in quantizing gravity. Some of the conceptual challenges like the meaning

2.5 Algebra of Constraints

The appearance of constraints, which generate gauge symmetries, is, as one can

expert, a general feature of systems with gauge symmetries. The group structure

of gauge transformations is reflected in the algebra of constraints, in particular

by the fact that the Poisson brackets between constraints is again a combination

of constraints. If this is the case for a given set of constraints, it will be called

first class [10]. However not all constraints are related by gauge symmetries, in

particular there are second class constraints, for which the Poisson brackets do

not vanish on the constraint hypersurface. In what follows, we try to examine if

the constraints (2.40) are first class constraints, and of particular interest to us

of these Poisson bracket algebras, are whether if they completely determine the

theory.

Space Variables

The choice of a basic set of phase space function {f} is an integral part of canonical

quantization. This set is promoted into operators {f̂} on some kinematical Hilbert

space. By promoting the set into operators, they should map Poisson brackets into

commutators, i.e

[f̂ , ĝ] = i~{f̂, g}. (3.1)

However, this basic set should be sufficiently large, so as to distinguish between

phase space points.

The result of the Poisson bracket between the diad and the spin connection at

the classical level gives a dirac delta function. At the quantum level, this delta

function has no equivalent proper operators. Hence one must smear the canonical

variables with an appropriate smooth and fast decaying function, in order to select

a proper set of the basic variables at the quantum level.

In selecting a proper set of the basic variable, the Poisson bracket between them

should result in a simple expression forming an algebra. By forming an algebra,

quantization of this basic set become feasible. Furthermore, one would like that the

phase space functions transform in a simple way under gauge transformations, so

that these can be implemented as gauge transformations in a kinematical Hilbert

space.

Subsequent discussions in this chapter will focus on the descretized form of the

spin connection and the diad, these form a basic set of the phase space function

to be quantized. Computation of the Poisson bracket between these basic set will

be carried out. The result will show a much simpler expression compared to the

Chapter 4

Kinematical Hilbert Space

The choice of the canonical variables have been found. We will now aim at a

canonical (Dirac) quantization of the system, this will also provide the tools to

derive a (covariant) path integral quantization. In defining a kinematical Hilbert

space of the system, we first find a representation of the phase space variables

as operators on some space of functions, introduce the notion of a cylindrical

functions (space of functions of operators), after which we equip this cylindrical

functions with an inner product. This allows us to find an orthonormal basis for

the cylindrical functions.

Chapter 5

Dynamics

The spinfoam approach of quantum gravity aims at constructing a rigorous well

defined mathematical notion of path integral for LQG as a tool for solving the

dynamics of the theory [19]. Characterization of the kernel of the quantum con-

straints of the theory given by quantization of the classical constraints of general

relativity defines the dynamics. The aim of these spinfoam models is to explicitly

construct a generalized projection operator from Hkin into the kernel of quantum

scalar constraint.

In [19], the authors establish a clear cut link between the spin foam approach and

the canonical quantization of three dimensional gravity. This they achieved by

constructing a physical scalar product (matrix element) of a regularized projector

operator which can be represented in terms of sum of finite spin foam amplitudes.

In this present work, we make a link between these approaches (i.e. spin foam and

canonical quantization), and to understand how the time gauge procedure from

SU(2) to SO(2) works at the quantum level. Essentially, we want to solve the

dynamics of our theory, by first constructing the matrix element of the projector

P on the physical Hilbert space.

In chapter 4, a kinematical Hilbert space of the theory in terms of the holonomies

was defined. And this can be seen as a first step towards understanding the

quantum geometry [17] of spin foams and its link to canonical formalism. In the

long run, the goal is to have a spin foam approach whose boundary states have an

SO(2) invariant spin networks.

Chapter 6

Conclusion and Outlook

In this thesis, we time gauge fix the three dimensional Hilbert-Palatini action and

got some new physics resulting from the canonical analysis.

The triad is decomposed into its various components via the time gauge (2.27). In

addition, we applied the triad decomposition to carry out a canonical analysis on

the Hilbert-Palatini action. The diad and the spin connection (two dimensions)

emerge as the new dynamical variables of the new theory.

By time gauge fixing the Hilbert-Palatini action, the usual constraints associated

to an action upon a canonical analysis is carried are obtain, thus the Gauss,

the spatial diffeomorphism and the Hamiltonian constraints. However, a new

constraint, i.e., C also emerges. In computing the time evolution associated with

the Gauss constraint G, the new theory generates an internal rotation in two

dimensions. Additionally, diffeomorphism invariance is achieved from the time

evolution associated with the spatial diffeomorphism constraint V .

In computing the algebra of constraints for the constraints of the new theory,

we found out the new theory was consistent and closed, in the sense that all

the Poisson brackets between the different constraints vanish on the constraint

hypersurface. The gauge transformation of the new system is an SO(2) gauge

transformation.

In chapter 3, a descretized form of the new dynamical variables is defined. These

form a basic set of the phase space function to be quantized. The Poisson bracket

between these basic set result in a much simpler expression compared to the non-

descretized will be carried out. The result shows a much simpler expression com-

pared to the non-descretized version of the canonical variables.

A kinematical Hilbert space is constructed for the new theory with an SO(2) spin

network. In carry out quantization the new theory we follow a similar approach

55

University of Ghana                              http://ugspace.ug.edu.gh



in [19]. We constructed a rigorous definition of a generalized projection operator

from the kinematical Hilbert space. In addition, we provided the definition of the

physical scalar product (matrix element) of the projection operator. This matrix

element represents a sum over finite spin-foam amplitudes. As a result a very

trivial spinfoam is obtained as compared to the Ponzano-Regge spinfoam model.

This trivial spinfoam model has SO(2) spin networks as it boundaries. However in

the Ponzano-Regge spinfoam model [27], there is a contraction of four 3j-symbols

(associated to a trivalent spin network) which results in a function of six spins

{j1, j2, j3, j4, j5, j6} with the faces bounded by the vertex of a tetrahedron. This

new function is the Wigner 6j-symbol.

Appendix A

ADM Decomposition of 2 + 1

Gravity

The unification of space and time play a crucial role in general relativity. Physi-

cally, general relativity is the discovery that spacetime and gravitational field are

the same entity. What we call “spacetime” is itself a physical object in many

respects similar to the electromagnetic field. This led to the discovery that there

is no spacetime at all, and so what Newton called “space” and Minkowski called

“spacetime” is nothing but a dynamical object called the gravitational field [27].

The Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) formalism however introduces an explicit- al-

though largely arbitrary division of spacetime into spatial and temporal divisions.

The decomposition of spacetime into space and time furnishes a natural setting

for the initial value problem, and it underlies Wheeler’s ’geometrodynamical’ pic-

ture of classical general relativity as the dynamics of evolving spatial geometries.

By providing a canonical description of the gravitational phase space, it leads

to a Hamiltonian version of classical gravity, and suggests a useful approach to

canonical quantization [5].

Representation Theory

B.1 Group Representation

Definition B.1.1. A finite dimensional representation of a Lie group G on a

vector space over a field K is a group homomorphism from G to GL(V ), the

general linear group on V . That is, a representation is a map [1]

φ : G −→ GL(V ) (B.1)

such that φ(g1g2) = φ(g1)φ(g2), for all g1, g2 ∈ G. The dimension of the represen-

tation is the dimension of the vector space V . Denote the representation of G in

V by (G, V ).

Definition B.1.2. Let (G, V ) be a representation. A subspace U of V is called

invariant or G-invariant if g.U ⊂ U for g ∈ G.

A representation (G, V ) has always at least two invariant subspaces, namely {0}
and V .

Definition B.1.3. A representation is called irreducible if the only invariant sub-

spaces are {0} and V .

B.2 Peter-Weyl Decomposition Theorem

Definition B.2.1. A matrix coefficient of a group G is a complex-valued function

ϕ on G given as the composition

ϕ = L ◦ π

where π is a finite-dimensional group representation of G, and L is a linear func-

tional on the vector space of the endomorphisms of V which contains GL(V ) as

an open subset.

The Peter-Weyl decomposition theorem is a theory of harmonic analysis, applying

to topological groups that are compact but not necessarily abelian. The theorem

is a collection of results generalizing the significant facts about the decomposition

of the regular representation of any finite group.

The theorem has three parts: (i) The set of matrix coefficients of a group G is

dense in the space of continuous complex functions onG equipped with the uniform

norm. (ii) Let ρ be a unitary representation of a compact group G on a complex

Hilbert space H. Then H splits into an orthogonal direct sum of irreducible

finite dimensional unitary representation of G. (iii) The matrix coefficients for G,

suitably renormalized, are an orthonormal basis of the square integrable functions

of G (L2(G)). In particular, L2(G) decomposes into an orthogonal direct sum of

all the irreducible unitary representations.

abstracts.value:
In this work, we review 3-dimensional gravity by canonically analyzing the HilbertPalatini action. We apply a time gauge used in 4-dimensional loop quantum gravity [14] to the simpler case of the 3-dimensional loop quantum gravity. By time
gauge fixing this Hilbert-Palatini action it leads to the Gauss constraints, the spatial diffeomorphism constraints, the Hamiltonian constraint and a new constraintC. The gauge symmetries generated by this new constraints are spacetime diffeomorphism and SO(2) gauge transformations. We solve the dynamics of the theory
by providing a regularization of the generalized projector operator in terms of the
Hamiltonian constraint. We provide the definition of the physical scalar product
which can be represented in terms of a sum over finite spinfoam amplitudes. Then
we establish a clear-cut link between the canonical quantization of the new theory
to the spinfoam model (Ponzano-Regge model) defined in terms of the SU (2) spin
networks.

titles.title: Time Gauge Fixing for 3d Loop Quantum Gravity

abstracts.value: Selecting an effective quantum compiler configuration requires coordinated decisions over both hardware targets and compiler settings, with the ultimate goal of improving circuit execution fidelity. Existing SOTA approaches typically decompose this problem into two sequential stages: a device is chosen first, after which compiler options are tuned on that device through RL-based search. This bottom-up strategy can be fundamentally limited by its initial device decision, since a poorly matched backend may constrain the best fidelity achievable regardless of how effectively later compiler options are optimized. In contrast to classical compiler tuning, where the search space is often prohibitively large, the configuration space of quantum compilers remains manageable enough to support exhaustive search. Consequently, rather than repeatedly searching from candidate configurations, one can derive reusable configuration knowledge from offline oracle results and apply it directly to new circuits. In this paper, we introduce a top-down configuration-selection paradigm and build QuOPTBench, an exhaustively searched benchmark containing oracle configurations for 268 quantum circuits. We first study whether LLMs can directly infer suitable configurations and evaluate ten representative LLMs. The results reveal that vanilla LLMs remain far from the oracle. We then employ an LLM to extract transferable rules from sampled circuits governing configuration selection. Using these rules together with predictors trained on the enumerated configuration data of the sampled circuits, we design QuTOP, a rule-guided ML framework that performs fast configuration selection without iterative online search. Across our evaluation, the distilled rules consistently strengthen LLM-based selection, while QuTOP provides the strongest overall balance between solution quality and selection latency among the baselines.

titles.title: Turning Quantum Compiler Configuration Selection Upside Down: A Top-Down Paradigm

abstracts.value: A quantum computer could recover the key of any Ethereum account whose public key appears on chain. We prove that no sidechain or bridge that leaves Ethereum's rules unchanged can protect such accounts: their funds must move into a contract whose release condition relies only on quantum-safe primitives. We design \emph{PQ-Vault}, a custody system for unmodified Ethereum combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain whose checkpoints carry compact certificates, and an optimistic dispute protocol. We give the first security proof of compact certificates against quantum attackers and a matching attack: with classically chosen parameters, the guarantee falls from 128 to about 60 bits, and a simple rule restores it. We show that a common seed-update rule in hash-chain proof of stake lets an attacker steer chosen slots and profit from splitting its stake, and give an election whose steering gain and inclusion delay are provably bounded against quantum attackers. Since compressing certificates with a pairing-based SNARK breaks quantum security, we use fraud proofs that need a single signature check. For 65,536 validators, a certificate is 0.8 MB, 260 times smaller than all signatures, and verifies in about 20 ms; the vault accepts a checkpoint for about 420,000 gas.

titles.title: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum

abstracts.value: Jet tagging is one of the most important applications of machine learning at the Large Hadron Collider. Recent models build in more physics knowledge or rely on large-scale pretraining, but the experiments place strict limits on their inference cost. Knowledge distillation can transfer their performance to small students that are cheap to run. We ask which properties of a teacher help the student, how small a student can get and how close it can come to the state of the art. On a jet tagging benchmark, we distil six teachers that differ in architecture, symmetry and pretraining, including two foundation models, into five small students. Every teacher improves every student, and the gain depends mainly on the strength of the teacher. We then shrink our two strongest distilled students, Transformer and L-GATr-slim, in width and in depth. With 20 thousand parameters, a distilled L-GATr-slim outperforms every published jet tagger trained from scratch at a fraction of the inference cost of every teacher. Even with two thousand parameters, it matches ParT, a model with a thousand times as many parameters. We also study what the students learn from their teachers. Our benchmark of inference cost shows that students of the same size can differ by almost an order of magnitude in speed. We release the code and the weights of all trained models.

titles.title: How Far Can Foundation Models Be Distilled for Efficient Jet Tagging?

abstracts.value: The same classical f-divergence admits inequivalent extensions to quantum states. The question is whether these extensions can be obtained from a common classical variational principle with an operational interpretation. Here we generalize Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization by introducing retrodictive tests relative to a reference state. A retrodictive test compares a forward and a reverse stochastic process, realized by quantum preparation and measurement, related by Petz transposition relative to the chosen reference, and subject to prescribed quantum averages. Equivalently, it compares two reverse tests sharing a reference output, whose labels are coupled by retrodiction. For faithful states in finite dimension, we prove that the same spectral implementation attains the minimum classical f-divergence over all admissible implementations simultaneously for every operator-convex f. A flat reference yields the standard quantum f-divergences, thereby giving the Nussbaum-Szkoła distributions a variational characterization. Choosing either prescribed state as reference recovers maximal quantum f-divergences and Matsumoto's reverse-test optimization, while power references interpolate between the standard and maximal divergences along the geodesic family. In the relative-entropy case, this gives the passage from Umegaki to Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy by changing the reference state. The same optimization extends to arbitrary quantum channels and, for channels with faithful Choi operator, gives a variational characterization of quantum entropy production.

titles.title: Quantum f-divergences from retrodictive tests: a unifying classical variational principle
