At this point it is important to notice that the subset of MG
models we are considering only hold in the linear regime,
which we assume to be the one valid inside solar-type stars
(and other high-density stars such as WDs). In this sense, we
must emphasize that some proposed modifications of gravity
on cosmological scales that rely on screening mechanisms
(Koyama & Sakstein 2015; Saito et al. 2015) through nonlinear
effects on astrophysical scales are not covered by this
approach.
Notice that because of the form of the effective operator μ,

the structure of the pressure equation is different from that
shown in Equation (1). A few comments are in order. For
simplicity we have limited ourselves to the case in which the
parameters p3, p4, and p5 are just object-independent constants.
In the most general case, for the spherically symmetric
configurations considered in the work and unlike the
cosmological case discussed in Silvestri et al. (2013), these
parameters could be general functions of the stellar radius.
Thus, for example, the p4 parameter related to the effective
Newton’s constant could interpolate between different values
in the interior and exterior of the star. However, in our case
with constant p4, matching with the laboratory-measured value
of Newton constant G imposes p4=1. Thus, the combination
G/p4 appearing in the obtained structure equations inside the
stellar body will effectively take the value G. The possibility of
changing the effective Newton’s constant in astrophysical
objects as compared to the laboratory value has been
considered phenomenologically in previous works in non-
weak-field limits; see, for instance, Velten et al. (2016) and
references therein, where an α parameter is used analogously to
our p4 or in cosmological contexts, and see Planck Collabora-
tion et al. (2016) for explicit measurements of μ0.

4. Conclusions

Using a model-independent approach, we have studied the
effects of a subset of MG theories involving one extra scalar
degree of freedom on stellar structure. We use a perturbative
technique capable of solving in a linearized regime. We have
selected our main scenario concerning the application to low-
density stellar objects. First, in a perturbative approach, we
have obtained mass and radius solutions for low-mass solar-
type objects using a polytropic n=3 EoS. We have analyzed
how internal temperature profiles and stellar luminosities are
affected with respect to the reference case of GR. We provide a
fit for masses and radii provided a central density value, i.e.,
M(ξ, ρc), R(ξ, ρc). We obtain that a change in the curvature of
M(R) results when ξ changes from positive to negative values,
connecting the latter to metastable stellar configurations. We
also find that MG can affect stellar luminosity from its
ξ dependence. Globally, the effective temperature from a
µL Teff

4 law results in a linear Log L–Log Teff behavior with a
weak dependence on ξ. We anticipate that this could result in
objects appearing brighter (as L is increased with any stable
configuration ξ>0, but this seems hard to measure experi-
mentally as internal stellar dynamics is complex. Furthermore,
it seems challenging to disentangle this effect from other
standard effects such as proper fluctuations of the star. Even the
Sun is a weakly variable star, with its major source of
fluctuation coming from the 11-year solar cycle and revealing a
smaller periodic variation of about ∼±0.1%. It is nevertheless
worth pointing out that both effects, involving standard and
new physics, could indeed be present and need to be further
studied. When a particular case of a high-density star is
considered (WDs), we find that no constraint appears on the
ξ parameter from calculated values of the Chandrasekhar mass

as it is always larger than the GR value in the perturbative
approach we use. Our treatment for both low- and high-density
stellar case examples can help to understand the behavior of
MG on small (not cosmological) scales.

abstracts.value: The collaboration between NVIDIA and Fermilab will create a high-bandwidth data processing pipeline which uses state of the art Artificial Intelligence to analyze data generated by Fermilab’s DUNE. The collaboration will enable data generated by the experiment to be analyzed close to the source, reducing networking, storage, and time requirements for offline data analysis. The collaboration will analyze potential current and future hardware solutions enabling real‐time analysis of data, as well as performance analysis and improvements based on the LArCV2 codebase to support the performance of goals of the experiment and associated equipment.

Abstract

This thesis develops machine-learning methods for charged-particle tracking
and boosted Higgs-boson pair searches with the ATLAS experiment at the
Large Hadron Collider. Its primary focus is charged-particle reconstruction
in dense detector environments, motivated by the upgraded ATLAS Inner
Tracker at the High-Luminosity LHC.

Studies of high-pT bottom (b)-hadron decays within the conventional ATLAS
tracking chain localise substantial e!ciency losses to track finding and
ambiguity resolution. Targeted modifications to individual reconstruction
requirements do not consistently recover these losses, motivating alternative
approaches based on learned detector-hit association.

A Transformer-based tracking architecture is introduced that formulates
reconstruction as set prediction with track-level hit-assignment masks. For
pixel-only reconstruction of particles with pT → 1 GeV, the best-performing
model achieves a combined hit-filter and tracking e!ciency of 98.1%, with
a fake rate of 0.3%, and processes an event in 63.7 ± 6.6 ms on a single
NVIDIA A100 GPU. Physics-informed modifications to the query con-
struction and cross-attention reduce computational cost and enable scaling
to lower transverse-momentum thresholds and heterogeneous pixel–strip
inputs.

Finally, three data-driven multijet background-estimation methods are
derived and compared for a boosted non-resonant HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ search using
Run 2 and partial Run 3 data. Validation studies favour the combined
Gaussian-process and conditional-flow approach. The signal region remains
blinded, and no final statistical interpretation is presented.

Impact Statement

This thesis presents research in fundamental particle physics, with a focus on
machine-learning techniques for improving the reconstruction and interpre-
tation of proton–proton collision data recorded by the ATLAS experiment
at the Large Hadron Collider.

Precise measurements made using ATLAS data may reveal deviations from
Standard Model predictions and point towards a more complete descrip-
tion of fundamental physics. Such deviations could provide insight into
open questions including the nature of dark matter, the origin of the
matter–antimatter asymmetry, and the structure of the Higgs sector. These
measurements depend on our ability to accurately reconstruct particles
from detector signals and distinguish rare Higgs processes from much larger
backgrounds. This thesis contributes to that e"ort through development of
machine-learning methods for both charged-particle tracking and boosted
Higgs-boson pair searches.

Particle physics seeks to understand the origin, composition, and evolution of
the Universe. The pursuit of knowledge about the physical world is valuable
in its own right, while history has also shown that fundamental research can
have practical consequences far beyond those anticipated at the time. The
discovery of the electron, for example, helped provide the microscopic basis
for modern electronics. Additionally, particle-physics research has produced
and advanced technologies that have found broad societal application, with
work at CERN having contributed to developments including the World
Wide Web, medical accelerator and magnet technologies, advanced sensors,
distributed computing, and large-scale data processing.

A further complementary form of impact arises from the exchange of meth-
ods between particle physics and the wider machine-learning community.
Collider data present distinctive challenges, involving large, irregular, and
high-dimensional inputs, complex probability distributions, and weak signals

embedded in substantial backgrounds. Particle physics draws on machine-
learning and statistical methods to address these problems, while techniques
developed in this context can in turn inform other data-intensive fields.

This exchange is enabled by the collaborative and interdisciplinary structure
of modern particle physics. Experiments such as ATLAS bring together
thousands of researchers worldwide and provide training in machine learning,
statistics, high-performance computing, communication, and collaborative
problem solving. They develop highly skilled researchers with practical
expertise in applied artificial intelligence and large-scale data analysis,
capabilities that are increasingly valuable across the wider research landscape
and economy. Through publication, education, and public engagement, the
programme also contributes to a wider understanding both of fundamental
physics and of the scientific process.

Chapter 1

Introduction

A central aim of scientific research is to explain observed phenomena in terms of under-
lying principles. Particle physics pursues this aim by probing matter at the smallest
experimentally accessible distance scales, where the structure of the macroscopic world
is resolved into elementary particles, quantum fields, and fundamental interactions.
These interactions shaped the conditions of the early Universe and govern the behaviour
of matter today, making their study central to questions about the origin, composi-
tion, and evolution of the Universe. Although ordinary matter emerges from these
constituents and interactions, their microscopic behaviour is governed by quantum
and relativistic principles that are far removed from our macroscopic experience of the
world.

In collider experiments, this microscopic behaviour is studied by accelerating beams
to high energies and bringing them into collision. The resulting interactions can
produce massive, short-lived particles, whose properties are inferred from the stable or
long-lived particles recorded by surrounding detectors. The particles and interactions
revealed through this experimental programme are described by the Standard Model
of particle physics, developed over the past century through sustained theoretical
and experimental progress. Its predictions have achieved remarkable agreement with
observation, and the discovery of the Higgs boson by the ATLAS and CMS experiments
in 2012 completed its known particle content and provided experimental confirmation
of the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking.

Despite this success, the Standard Model is not a complete description of nature. It
does not incorporate gravity, provide a viable particle candidate for cosmological dark
matter, or account for the observed matter–antimatter asymmetry through its known

14



Introduction 15

sources of CP violation. The origin of neutrino masses also lies outside its minimal
formulation, while the values of many of its parameters are measured experimentally
rather than predicted. Within the Higgs sector, interactions involving a single Higgs
boson have been measured with increasing precision, but the form of the scalar potential
remains only weakly tested. Precision measurements and searches for rare processes
therefore provide complementary means of probing the limits of the theory. Deviations
from Standard Model predictions could indicate additional particles, interactions, or
symmetries.

Progress on these questions depends not only on higher collision energies and larger
datasets, but also on the ability to extract reliable physical information from increasingly
complex detector signatures. At the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), rare processes
must be reconstructed from high-dimensional, sparse detector data and separated from
backgrounds that are many orders of magnitude larger. Higgs-boson pair production is a
central example, as it provides a direct collider probe of the trilinear Higgs self-coupling,
but must be distinguished from large backgrounds with similar detector signatures.

These challenges are naturally expressed as high-dimensional inference tasks. Collider
events are collections of detector measurements and reconstructed objects, from which
the properties of the underlying particles and processes must be inferred. Statistical
learning methods have long been used for such tasks in collider physics, while recent
developments in deep learning have expanded the ability to learn flexible reconstruction,
object-identification, and background-estimation models from high-dimensional detector
and event data. These methods provide new opportunities to improve both the accuracy
and computational e!ciency of collider reconstruction and analysis.

This thesis investigates how physically structured machine-learning methods can be
used to improve the extraction of physics information from ATLAS detector data.
The principal focus is charged-particle tracking. High-pT b-hadron decays in dense
jet environments expose limitations of the conventional reconstruction chain. These
limitations motivate a Transformer-based formulation in which tracks are reconstructed
as query-level hit-assignment masks, and the subsequent architectural development
to improve scalability towards High-Luminosity LHC occupancies and heterogeneous
detector inputs. Finally, machine-learning methods are applied at the analysis level to
data-driven multijet background estimation in a boosted HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ search.



Introduction 16

Together, these studies follow the flow of information from low-level detector measure-
ments to high-level physics inference. They examine how detector geometry, event
structure, and physical constraints can be incorporated into machine-learning mod-
els to improve reconstruction e!ciency, computational scalability, and the statistical
separation of rare Higgs-boson processes from background.

This thesis is organised as follows.

Chapter 2 introduces the theoretical foundations of the work. It summarises the
Standard Model, the Higgs mechanism and electroweak symmetry breaking, Higgs-
boson production and decay at the LHC, and the role of Higgs-boson pair production
as a direct probe of the Higgs self-interaction.

Chapter 3 introduces the experimental context for this work, including the LHC, the
ATLAS detector, and the upgraded Inner Tracker planned for the High-Luminosity
LHC. Chapter 4 then reviews the reconstruction of physics objects from ATLAS
detector signals, with emphasis on charged-particle tracking, flavour tagging, and
machine-learning representations of variable-size collider data.

Chapter 5 investigates tracking ine!ciencies for charged particles produced in high-pT

b-hadron decays. The study indicates that the surrounding dense charged-particle
environment is an important contributor to the degradation. Substantial losses are
observed during both track finding and ambiguity resolution and are di!cult to recover
through local modifications of individual stages, motivating learned approaches based
on direct detector-hit association.

Chapter 6 then introduces a MaskFormer-inspired approach in which charged-particle
reconstruction is formulated as query-based set prediction from detector hits. Chapter 7
builds on this formulation by developing dynamic-query and sparse-attention methods
to improve reconstruction performance and computational scalability, and extends the
study to lower transverse-momentum thresholds and pixel–strip detector inputs.

Chapter 8 presents the development of a boosted non-resonant HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ analysis
using Run 2 and partial Run 3 data. The chapter describes the event selection, Higgs-
tagging strategy, analysis regions, and data-driven multijet background estimation,
including baseline rescaling, classifier-based reweighting, and a probabilistic model
based on Gaussian processes and conditional normalising flows.

The principal conclusions are summarised in Chapter 9.



Chapter 2

Theory

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics describes all known elementary particles
and their interactions, excluding gravity, within the framework of quantum field
theory. Over decades, it has predicted phenomena ranging from electroweak precision
observables to the properties of the top quark, achieving an unprecedented level of
agreement with experiment.

The discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012 confirmed the mechanism by which particles
acquire mass and completed the model’s particle content [1, 2]. However, the structure
of the Higgs sector is still poorly constrained. The scalar potential and the Higgs
self-coupling have not yet been measured directly, and current LHC results provide
only weak bounds [3–5]. Rare processes, such as Higgs-boson pair production, o"er a
unique window into these properties, providing sensitive tests of the Standard Model
and potential hints of physics beyond it.

This chapter presents the theoretical background necessary to interpret the analyses in
this thesis. It does not aim to provide full derivations, but focuses on the elements of
the SM and Higgs physics most relevant to this work. Particular emphasis is placed on
the Higgs sector and Higgs-boson pair production, which form a core motivation for
the analyses presented.

Section 2.1 introduces the Standard Model and its gauge structure, Section 2.2 describes
the Higgs mechanism and mass generation, Section 2.3 reviews Higgs production and
decay at the LHC, and Section 2.4 summarises the experimental status and motivates
ongoing studies of Higgs interactions.

Theory 18

2.1 The Standard Model of Particle Physics

The SM is formulated within relativistic quantum field theory, where particles are
excitations of underlying fields [6–8]. Its structure is determined by local gauge
symmetries and a small set of experimentally measured parameters. The following
subsections summarise the particle content and gauge interactions that underpin the
Standard Model and its predictions for collider phenomenology.

The particle content of the SM is summarised in Table 2.1. The matter sector consists
of spin-1/2 fermions arranged in three generations of quarks and leptons, with identical
gauge quantum numbers but di"erent masses. Each fermion has a corresponding
antiparticle. The bosonic sector contains the gauge bosons mediating the fundamental
interactions: the photon (ω) for electromagnetism, the eight gluons (g) for the strong
interaction, and the weak bosons (W±, Z) for the charged- and neutral-current weak
interactions. The scalar Higgs boson (H) arises from the Higgs field and is associated
with electroweak symmetry breaking and the generation of particle masses [8–11].

The SM describes the strong, electromagnetic, and weak interactions. These interactions
are dictated by local gauge invariance under [12–15] SU(3)C ↓ SU(2)L ↓U(1)Y , where
SU(3)C describes the colour interaction of quarks and gluons, while SU(2)L ↓ U(1)Y

defines the electroweak sector. The structure of this gauge group fixes the allowed
interactions and determines the associated gauge fields. After electroweak symmetry

hadrons, while gravity is not included in the SM.

Gauge symmetries and interactions

In quantum field theory, symmetries determine interaction structure and conservation
laws. Global symmetries lead to conserved quantities via Noether’s theorem, while local
symmetries require the introduction of gauge fields, which mediate interactions [12, 16].

The aim of this chapter is not to rederive the full Standard Model Lagrangian, but to
summarise the theoretical ingredients most relevant for the remainder of this thesis.
The following sections therefore emphasise the gauge structure of the Standard Model,

Gauge invariance fixes the form of interactions through the introduction of covari-

Gauge theories are classified as Abelian or non-Abelian. In the renormalisable Abelian

such as confinement and asymptotic freedom in QCD [12,18,19].

Gauge invariance forbids explicit mass terms for gauge bosons, implying they are
massless unless the symmetry is broken. In the SM, this explains the massless photon
and the massive W

± and Z bosons following electroweak symmetry breaking [10,11,17].

2.2 The Higgs Mechanism

2.2.1 Motivation for Electroweak Symmetry Breaking

Although the electroweak gauge structure introduced above fixes the interactions of
the gauge fields and fermions, it does not by itself explain the observed spectrum of
particle masses. In the unbroken gauge theory, explicit gauge-boson mass terms of the
form

The Higgs mechanism provides a minimal resolution. A scalar field acquires a non-zero

in longitudinal gauge-boson scattering.

The predictive structure of the Higgs sector makes precision Higgs measurements a

2.3.2 Higgs-Boson Pair Production

Single-Higgs production tests the couplings of one Higgs boson to Standard Model
particles, but constrains the Higgs potential only indirectly. Higgs-boson pair production
provides the principal direct collider probe of the Higgs self-interaction. At the LHC,
non-resonant Higgs-boson pair production proceeds predominantly through gluon–
gluon fusion. At leading order, this process receives contributions from two classes of
diagrams. This is shown schematically in Fig. 2.3. In the triangle contribution, an
o"-shell Higgs boson is produced through a heavy-quark loop and subsequently splits
into a Higgs-boson pair; in the box contribution, both Higgs bosons couple directly to
the loop. Both contributions depend on the top-quark Yukawa coupling, while only
the triangle contribution depends directly on the trilinear Higgs self-coupling. In the
Standard Model, the two amplitudes interfere destructively, substantially suppressing
the total production rate.

the reconstruction and identification of heavy-flavour jets in a challenging multijet
environment. In boosted topologies, the decay products of each Higgs boson become
collimated and can be reconstructed within large-radius jets. These selections target
high-mHH phase space, where sensitivity to some deviations from the Standard Model
may be enhanced, and are complementary to resolved analyses. They also place
stringent requirements on tracking and heavy-flavour identification inside dense jets.
This motivates both the tracking studies and the boosted HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ analysis presented
in the remainder of this thesis.

ATLAS is a general-purpose detector located at one of the four primary LHC interaction

3.2.1 Inner Detector / Inner Tracking System

The Inner Detector is responsible for precision reconstruction of charged-particle
trajectories and interaction vertices within |▷| < 2.5. A charged-particle trajectory is
the path followed by a charged particle as it propagates through the detector material
and magnetic field. A reconstructed charged-particle trajectory is referred to as a track.
Tracks are inferred from spatially localised detector measurements produced as charged
particles traverse the tracking layers, and provide estimates of the particle direction,
momentum, charge, and point of origin.



The ATLAS Experiment 42

A superconducting solenoid surrounding the Inner Detector generates a uniform 2 T
magnetic field parallel to the beam direction. Charged particles therefore follow helical
trajectories, allowing both the magnitude and sign of the momentum to be inferred
from the track curvature.

The Inner Detector comprises three complementary subsystems arranged in concentric
layers around the beam pipe: the silicon pixel detector, the silicon strip tracker (SCT),
and the Transition Radiation Tracker (TRT). Looking ahead to the HL-LHC, this
system will be replaced by the all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk), designed for substantially
higher radiation levels and pile-up. An overview of the Inner Detector geometry is
shown in Figure 3.6.

Pixel Detector

The silicon pixel detector is the innermost component of the ATLAS Inner Detector and
provides the highest spatial resolution measurements for charged-particle tracking. Its
proximity to the interaction point makes it the dominant contributor to the precision
with which charged-particle trajectories are extrapolated back towards the collision
point. This is particularly important for reconstructing displaced decay topologies from
heavy-flavour hadrons.

The detector has a barrel–endcap geometry, with four cylindrical barrel layers and four
disk-shaped layers on each side of the interaction point. The innermost barrel layer
is the Insertable B-Layer (IBL), installed between Run 1 and Run 2 at a radius of
approximately 33 mm [42,43]. The remaining barrel pixel layers are located at radii of
approximately 50.5, 88.5, and 122.5 mm [31,42, 43]. This configuration provides up to
four high-precision space-point measurements per track within |▷| < 2.5.

In its original Run 1 configuration, the pixel detector consisted of three barrel layers
and three endcap disks on each side, comprising about 80 million channels with pixel
dimensions of 50 ↓ 400 µm

further channels with finer 50 ↓ 250 µm

Silicon Strip Tracker

Surrounding the pixel detector, the SCT provides high-precision measurements at inter-

comprises approximately 6.3 million readout channels, with strip pitches of order 80 µm

and lengths of several centimetres. Tracks traversing the full SCT typically accumulate
four additional space-points, corresponding to eight strip hits. Together with the
pixel detector, the SCT provides the core precision measurements used for momentum
determination and pattern recognition.

Transition Radiation Tracker

The TRT is the outermost component of the Inner Detector, with a sensitive barrel
region spanning approximately R = 563–1066 mm [31]. It is based on 4 mm diameter
straw-tube drift chambers, providing additional tracking measurements and electron

to approximately |▷| < 2.0, compared with |▷| < 2.5 for the pixel and SCT systems.
Each straw contains a central anode wire and operates as a proportional drift tube. In
total, the TRT comprises approximately 420 000 readout channels.

A typical track within the TRT acceptance produces about 30–40 TRT hits. Although
less precise than the silicon subsystems, the TRT extends the tracking lever arm and
contributes significantly to Run 1–3 tracking. It will be replaced by an all-silicon
system in the ITk upgrade.

3.2.3 Muon Spectrometer

The muon spectrometer is the outermost tracking subsystem and is dedicated to
muon identification and momentum measurement. It surrounds the calorimeter system
and extends to a radius of approximately 11 m in the barrel region. Since muons
lose relatively little energy in the calorimeters, they can be measured again in an
outer tracking system with a large lever arm, complementing the charged-particle
reconstruction from the Inner Detector.

Muon momenta are determined from the curvature of tracks in the magnetic field
produced by large superconducting air-core toroidal magnets located outside the
calorimeters. This toroidal field provides bending power for the muon spectrometer
while minimising the amount of material traversed by the muons. Precision tracking
is provided primarily by monitored drift tubes (MDTs) over most of the detector
acceptance. In the original Run 1 and Run 2 detector, cathode strip chambers (CSCs)
were used in the innermost forward regions, where particle rates are highest. For Run 3,
these stations were replaced by the New Small Wheel, which uses high-granularity
gaseous detectors designed to improve tracking and triggering in the forward region.
Fast trigger information is provided by resistive plate chambers (RPCs) in the barrel
and thin-gap chambers (TGCs) in the endcap regions, with the trigger chambers also
providing additional coordinate measurements complementary to the precision tracking
chambers.

The spectrometer provides precision tracking coverage up to |▷| < 2.7, while the muon
trigger system covers up to approximately |▷| < 2.4. For combined Inner Detector

3.2.4 Trigger and Data Acquisition

The bunch-crossing rate at the LHC is 40 MHz, far exceeding the rate at which events
can be permanently recorded for o#ine analysis. ATLAS therefore employs a trigger
and data acquisition (TDAQ) system to perform an online event selection in real time,
retaining events with signatures relevant for the physics programme while reducing
the data rate to a level compatible with permanent storage. During Run 2, the trigger
system recorded physics collisions at an average rate of approximately 1 kHz, while
in Run 3 the upgraded system can record up to about 3 kHz of fully built physics
events [46,47]. An overview of the TDAQ flow is shown in Figure 3.7.

L1 Trigger. The first-level trigger is a hardware-based system that uses reduced-
granularity information from the calorimeters and muon spectrometer to identify
high-pT signatures such as muons, electrons, photons, jets, hadronically decaying ϑ

leptons, and large missing transverse momentum. It reduces the rate from the 40 MHz
bunch-crossing rate to at most approximately 100 kHz, with a fixed latency below
2.5 µs, and defines regions of interest for later trigger stages.

High-Level Trigger. The High-Level Trigger (HLT) is software-based and runs on
a dedicated computing farm. Using detector information from the regions of interest
identified by L1, or from the full detector where required, it performs increasingly
refined reconstruction and selection using algorithms closely related to those used



The ATLAS Experiment 48

o#ine. The HLT reduces the accepted event rate to approximately 1 kHz in Run 2 and
up to about 3 kHz for fully built physics events in Run 3, after which selected events
are written to permanent storage for o#ine processing.

3.3.3 Reconstruction Challenges at the High-Luminosity LHC

The increased detector granularity of the ITk is designed to preserve tracking per-
formance under the substantially higher occupancies expected at the HL-LHC. Nev-
ertheless, the large number of simultaneous proton–proton interactions will increase
the density of detector measurements, the number of candidate trajectories, and the
frequency of ambiguous hit associations. These conditions place stringent demands on
both the accuracy and computational e!ciency of event reconstruction.

The following chapter describes how ATLAS detector measurements are transformed

Chapter 4

Event Reconstruction

Event reconstruction is the process by which raw detector signals recorded by the
ATLAS experiment are transformed into a structured description of the underlying
proton–proton interaction. This description is expressed in terms of reconstructed
physics objects such as tracks, vertices, jets, leptons, and missing transverse momentum.
The performance of this reconstruction chain directly determines the sensitivity of
measurements and searches at the Large Hadron Collider.

At a conceptual level, event reconstruction may be viewed as an inverse problem. In the
forward description, the products of a hard proton–proton collision propagate outwards
from the interaction point, traversing successive layers of detector material, as illustrated
in Fig. 4.1. Charged particles ionise the inner tracking detectors, electromagnetic and
hadronic showers develop in the calorimeters, and penetrating muons reach the outer
spectrometer, giving rise to low-level detector signals such as hits and energy deposits
recorded by the data acquisition system.

Reconstruction seeks to invert this mapping, inferring from discretised and imperfect
detector measurements the trajectories, kinematic properties, and identities of the
particles produced in the original interaction. This inverse problem is intrinsically
ambiguous, the recorded signals have finite resolution and granularity, may be a"ected
by instrumental noise, and can overlap when particles are produced close together in
dense final states. The interpretation is further complicated by secondary interactions in
the detector material, such as multiple scattering, bremsstrahlung, photon conversions,
and hadronic interactions, as well as by additional activity from pile-up proton–proton
collisions.

4.1.2 Track Parameterisation

The trajectory of a reconstructed charged particle in the Inner Detector is described
by a helix, reflecting its motion in the approximately uniform solenoidal magnetic field.
In the absence of material interactions, the helical curvature in the transverse plane is
determined by the particle’s transverse momentum and electric charge. In practice,
each track is parameterised by five quantities, defined at the point of closest approach

Two parameters describe the displacement of the track from the reference point. The

The fitted track parameters are accompanied by a covariance matrix, which encodes

4.2 Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction

Charged-particle track reconstruction is a foundational component of event recon-
struction in the ATLAS experiment. Reconstructed tracks are used throughout the
reconstruction chain, either directly in the definition of physics objects or indirectly
through requirements on their presence or absence. They provide essential inputs to
vertex reconstruction, pile-up mitigation, jet reconstruction, lepton and photon identifi-
cation, missing transverse momentum reconstruction, and heavy-flavour identification.

Charged particles produced in a proton–proton collision traverse the Inner Detector,
leaving spatially localised measurements in the tracking subsystems. In the silicon
detectors, charge deposits are clustered and converted into space-points, while the
Transition Radiation Tracker provides additional drift-time measurements. Track
reconstruction associates these measurements into coherent trajectories and estimates
the corresponding track parameters.

The ATLAS track reconstruction procedure consists of several algorithmic stages:
space-point formation, seed finding, track finding and fitting, and ambiguity resolution.
Each stage is designed to balance reconstruction e!ciency, fake-track rejection, and

As a charged particle traverses the silicon sensors of the Inner Detector, it deposits
charge by ionisation. The deposited charge may be collected on more than one
readout channel, either because the particle crosses multiple pixels or strips or because
the charge drifts and di"uses before collection. In the pixel detector, neighbouring

clusters, as illustrated in Fig. 4.5. These clusters provide three-dimensional space-point

Pixel clusters and strip space-points provide a sparse and discretised sampling of the
underlying particle trajectory and form the primary inputs to silicon-seeded track
reconstruction.

The Transition Radiation Tracker provides additional measurements from drift times
in straw tubes. These measurements extend the tracking lever arm and can be used to
refine track candidates reconstructed in the silicon detectors.

4.2.2 Seed Finding

The first stage of pattern recognition is seed finding, which generates initial track
hypotheses from small groups of silicon space-points. Seeds are typically constructed
from triplets of space-points in the pixel or silicon strip detectors. Space-point triplets
that are geometrically compatible with a charged-particle trajectory in the solenoidal
magnetic field are retained as candidate seeds and passed to the subsequent track-finding
stage.

Loose selection criteria are applied at this stage, including constraints on curvature
and impact parameter, in order to suppress unphysical combinations while maintaining
high e!ciency. Multiple seeds may be formed for a single underlying particle, ensuring
robustness against missing or mis-measured hits.



Event Reconstruction 58

For accepted triplets, an additional confirmation space-point is searched for on a distinct
detector layer. The presence of a confirmation space-point with compatible curvature
provides further evidence that the seed corresponds to a genuine particle trajectory
and is used as an input to later quality assessment.

4.2.3 Track Finding and Fitting

For each seed, an initial estimate of the track parameters is used to extrapolate the
candidate trajectory through the detector. The first stage of track finding involves
search-road building, in which the seed parameters are used to identify the set of
detector modules that the particle is expected to traverse. Seeds for which an insu!cient
number of compatible detector layers are found are discarded at this stage, reducing
the combinatorial complexity of subsequent reconstruction.

Track candidates are then built using a Combinatorial Kalman Filter [59, 60]. Starting
from the seed, the filter propagates the track state to successive detector layers, predicts
the expected measurement position, and updates the track parameters using compatible
space-points. Measurement uncertainties, multiple scattering, and energy loss in the
detector material are incorporated naturally within the Kalman formalism. In regions
of high occupancy, more than one compatible space-point may be found at a given layer.
The candidate is then branched, allowing multiple hit-assignment hypotheses to be
explored in parallel. This combination of iterative state estimation and combinatorial
hypothesis building is illustrated in Fig. 4.6.

The Kalman filter produces an estimate of the track parameters at each layer, together
with an associated covariance matrix. The quality of the fit can be assessed using
quantities such as the global ◁2 of the trajectory. The resulting set of fitted candidates
is then passed to the ambiguity-resolution stage, where competing candidates and
shared measurements are resolved.

The track-finding stage yields a collection of track candidates, many of which may share
space-points or represent alternative interpretations of the same underlying particle.

Each track candidate is assigned a score reflecting its compatibility with a well-

transverse momentum, the number and type of associated hits, the presence of holes,
the number of shared hits with other candidates, and the fit quality. Candidates are
then processed in order of decreasing score. At this stage, additional requirements
are applied to reject low-quality candidates and to resolve cases in which multiple
candidates share the same detector measurements. High-scoring candidates are therefore
preferentially retained, while candidates failing quality or hit-sharing criteria are rejected.
Representative quality requirements are summarised in Table 4.1.

The ambiguity solver proceeds iteratively through the scored candidate list. Candidates
are ordered in decreasing score, and the highest-scoring remaining candidate is con-
sidered first. For each candidate, the clusters already assigned to previously accepted
tracks are counted, and the candidate is tested against requirements on the number of
total and unique silicon clusters, the number of shared modules, and the number of
holes. A cluster is considered shared only with respect to tracks that have already been
accepted. If a candidate uses clusters beyond the allowed sharing limits, those clusters
may be removed from the candidate; the candidate is rejected if the resulting track fails
the required quality criteria. Once a candidate is accepted, its cluster content is fixed
and cannot be modified by later, lower-scoring candidates. Candidates that satisfy the
cluster-sharing and quality requirements are passed to the global ◁2 fitter, which refines
the track parameters and may identify outlier measurements. The fitted candidate is
then re-scored, including its fit quality, and returned to the ambiguity-solver input list.
If, on a subsequent pass, it still satisfies the ambiguity-resolution requirements without
further modification, it is added to the final collection of resolved tracks [56].

The output of this procedure is a collection of resolved tracks with fitted parameters
suitable for use in downstream reconstruction algorithms.

4.3 Physics Objects

The tracks, calorimeter energy deposits, and muon-system measurements reconstructed
from the detector readout are combined to form the physics objects used in analysis.
These objects include primary vertices, jets, electrons, photons, muons, and missing
transverse momentum. They provide a compact description of the event in terms of
experimentally measurable quantities that can be related to the particles produced in
the proton–proton collision. The following sections summarise the main reconstructed
objects used throughout this thesis.

4.3.1 Primary Vertices

A vertex is defined as a point in space from which a set of reconstructed charged-particle
tracks is consistent with originating. In proton–proton collisions, multiple interactions
can occur within the same bunch crossing, each giving rise to a distinct primary vertex.
Vertex reconstruction is therefore essential for identifying the hard-scatter interaction
of interest and for mitigating the impact of pile-up.

Primary-vertex reconstruction begins from a selected collection of reconstructed tracks
that are compatible with originating from the beam-collision region. These tracks are
required to satisfy quality criteria on the number of associated silicon measurements,
impact parameters with respect to the beam spot, and transverse momentum in order
to suppress fake or poorly measured tracks. Candidate vertex positions are seeded
from the distribution of selected tracks along the beam axis. The tracks are then fitted
to one or more vertex hypotheses using an adaptive vertex-fitting procedure, in which
tracks are assigned weights according to their compatibility with each vertex. Tracks
inconsistent with a given vertex hypothesis are down-weighted while the vertex position
is iteratively refined. In high pile-up conditions, where several interactions may occur
close together in z, the reconstruction must also separate nearby vertices and resolve
the association of tracks to competing interaction points [56, 63].

Among the reconstructed primary vertices, one is designated as the hard-scatter primary
vertex. This is usually defined as the vertex whose associated tracks maximise the
scalar sum of squared transverse momenta,

High pile-up increases the number of reconstructed interaction vertices in each event
and can produce vertices that are close together along the beam axis. This makes
both vertex separation and hard-scatter identification more di!cult, especially when
tracks from pile-up interactions are mis-associated or when the hard-scatter vertex has
relatively low track activity.

4.3.2 Jets

Jets arise as a consequence of colour confinement in quantum chromodynamics. Quarks
and gluons produced in high-energy proton–proton collisions undergo parton showering
and hadronisation, producing colour-neutral particles emitted in a collimated configu-
ration. The resulting spray of particles forms a jet whose combined four-momentum is
correlated with that of the initiating parton. A schematic illustration of this process is
shown in Fig. 4.7.

Figure 4.7: Schematic illustration of jet formation in proton–proton collisions. A high-energy
parton undergoes radiation and hadronisation, producing a collimated spray of particles that
is reconstructed as a jet. Reproduced from [64].

Jets are reconstructed by applying a clustering algorithm to a collection of detector-level
inputs. In ATLAS, small-radius jets are commonly reconstructed from calorimeter
topological clusters or particle-flow objects. Topological clusters group neighbouring
calorimeter cells with significant energy deposits, using noise-suppression criteria to
build three-dimensional representations of calorimeter showers [65]. Particle-flow



Event Reconstruction 63

reconstruction combines Inner Detector tracks with calorimeter clusters, using the track
momentum for charged particles where it provides better resolution and subtracting
the corresponding calorimeter energy to avoid double counting [66]. Large-radius jets
may also be reconstructed from unified flow objects, which combine calorimeter- and
tracking-based information to improve performance over a broad kinematic range [67].

Jets are commonly reconstructed in ATLAS using the anti-kt algorithm [68]. This is a
sequential recombination algorithm in which inputs are iteratively combined according
to distance measures defined from their transverse momenta and angular separation.
It produces jets with stable, approximately conical boundaries in the ▷–↽ plane. The
characteristic angular scale of the jet is set by the radius parameter R. In ATLAS,
small-radius jets are commonly reconstructed with R = 0.4, while large-radius jets are
commonly reconstructed with R = 1.0 [69, 70].

The reconstructed jet four-momentum is defined from the four-momenta of its con-
stituents and is subsequently calibrated to correct for the detector response, energy
lost in inactive material, non-compensation of the calorimeter response, and additional
activity from pile-up [69,70]. Pile-up contributes extra particles and di"use calorimeter
energy deposits to the event, which can bias the reconstructed jet energy and increase
the probability of overlaps between reconstructed objects. Jet calibration and pile-up
mitigation are therefore essential components of jet reconstruction, particularly in
high-luminosity running conditions.

In simulated events, reconstructed jets are assigned flavour labels using particle-level
heavy-flavour hadrons associated with the jet. A jet is labelled as a b-jet if it is
associated with a b-hadron; if no b-hadron is present but a c-hadron is associated with
the jet, it is labelled as a c-jet. Jets associated with neither are classified as light-
flavour. These labels provide a reference for the flavour-tagging algorithms discussed
in Section 4.3.3.

4.3.3 Flavour Tagging

Beyond reconstructing their kinematic properties, many analyses require information
about the flavour of jets or their compatibility with the hadronic decay of a heavy
particle. The identification of jets containing heavy-flavour hadrons is particularly
important for processes involving top quarks and Higgs bosons, which frequently



Event Reconstruction 64

produce b-quarks in the final state. Flavour tagging refers to the inference of whether
a reconstructed jet contains the decay products of a bottom or charm hadron, or is
instead initiated by a light-flavour quark or gluon, using information from the jet and
its associated constituents [71].

Heavy-flavour tagging exploits the characteristic decay properties of bottom and charm
hadrons. Bottom hadrons have lifetimes of approximately ϑ ∝ 1.5 ps, corresponding to a
proper decay length of cϑ ∝ 450 µm. When produced with substantial momentum, they
may therefore travel several millimetres before decaying. The principal weakly decaying
charm hadrons have shorter lifetimes of approximately 0.2–1.0 ps, corresponding to
proper decay lengths of approximately 60–310 µm. They can therefore also produce
displaced decay products. Tracks from heavy-flavour decays consequently tend to have
large impact parameters with respect to the primary vertex and may form displaced
secondary or tertiary vertices, including through cascade decays such as b ↑ c. Accurate
track and vertex reconstruction is therefore essential for e"ective flavour tagging.

The relationship between prompt and displaced tracks is illustrated schematically in
Fig. 4.8. Tracks produced in heavy-flavour decays are inconsistent with originating
from the primary interaction vertex but may be compatible with a common displaced
vertex. Their impact parameters, the properties of reconstructed secondary vertices,
and the kinematics of tracks associated with the jet provide complementary information
for distinguishing heavy-flavour jets from light-flavour jets.

Modern ATLAS flavour-tagging algorithms use machine-learning models to combine
low-level track, vertex, and jet information. Graph Neural Network and Transformer-
based architectures model correlations between tracks associated with a jet, allowing
heavy-flavour decay topology to be inferred from their collective properties [73, 74].
Similar constituent-based architectures are used to identify hadronically decaying
boosted particles in large-radius jets. The GN2X algorithm, used in the boosted
HH ↑ bb̄bb̄ analysis described in Chapter 8, distinguishes decays such as H ↑ bb̄ from
multijet and top-quark backgrounds [75].

4.3.4 Reconstruction of Electrons and Photons

Electrons and photons are reconstructed from energy deposits in the electromagnetic
calorimeter. Candidate electromagnetic objects are built from clusters of calorimeter

reconstructed from electromagnetic clusters without a matched prompt track, while
converted photons are identified using tracks or reconstructed conversion vertices

Electron reconstruction accounts for bremsstrahlung in the Inner Detector material
through dedicated track-refitting procedures, improving the momentum estimate and
the compatibility between the track and calorimeter cluster. Electron identification
uses variables describing the electromagnetic shower shape, hadronic leakage, track
quality, track–cluster matching, and, where available, transition-radiation information.
These inputs are combined in likelihood-based discriminants, from which identification
working points are defined. Typical prompt-electron selections also impose requirements
on pT, fiducial acceptance, detector-quality regions, impact-parameter compatibility
with the primary vertex, and isolation.



Event Reconstruction 66

Photon identification relies primarily on the lateral and longitudinal development of the
electromagnetic shower. Photon candidates are typically required to satisfy minimum
pT, fiducial-acceptance, identification, and isolation requirements, where the isolation
is corrected for pile-up and for the contribution of the photon candidate itself.

4.3.5 Reconstruction of Muons

Muons are reconstructed using information from the Inner Detector and the Muon
Spectrometer. Tracks or track segments are first reconstructed independently in the
Muon Spectrometer and then matched to Inner Detector tracks. Combined muons are
obtained from a global fit to the Inner Detector and Muon Spectrometer measurements,
accounting for the energy lost by the muon in the calorimeters.

Muon identification working points are defined using the consistency of the Inner
Detector and Muon Spectrometer measurements, the quality of the fitted track, and
the number and quality of precision muon hits. Typical analysis selections require
muons to satisfy minimum pT and detector-acceptance requirements, to be compatible
with the primary vertex, and, when prompt muons are targeted, to be isolated from
nearby track or calorimeter activity [78].

4.3.6 Missing Transverse Momentum

Missing transverse momentum provides sensitivity to particles that do not interact
with the detector, such as neutrinos. It is reconstructed as the negative vector sum of
the transverse momenta of calibrated physics objects in the event, including electrons,
photons, muons, hadronically decaying ϑ -leptons, and jets, supplemented by a soft term
constructed from low-momentum activity not associated with these hard objects [79].
Since pile-up adds di"use low-momentum activity that is not associated with the
hard-scatter interaction, the soft term is a major source of pile-up sensitivity. In the
commonly used track-based soft term, only tracks associated with the primary vertex
are included, reducing the contribution from pile-up interactions.

4.4 Machine Learning for Object Reconstruction

4.4.1 Motivation

The reconstruction procedures described in the preceding sections transform detector
measurements into increasingly abstract physics objects. Tracks are inferred from
sparse Inner Detector measurements, vertices from compatible sets of tracks, jets
from clustered calorimeter and particle-flow inputs, and leptons, photons, and missing
transverse momentum from combinations of tracking, calorimeter, and muon-system
information. Each stage compresses the detector readout into a representation more
directly related to the particles produced in the proton–proton collision.

Many of these tasks are pattern-recognition problems [62,80]. The detector provides
incomplete and discretised measurements of the underlying event, while the reconstruc-
tion algorithm must infer which measurements are related, which particles produced



Event Reconstruction 68

them, and which properties should be assigned to the resulting objects. Traditional
algorithms address this through sequences of specialised procedures based on geometri-
cal constraints, quality selections, and fitted parameters. These methods are physically
motivated and have been highly successful, but rely on hand-designed intermediate
representations and fixed decision rules.

The increasing complexity of LHC events makes such rules harder to optimise [50–52,62].
High pile-up increases detector occupancy and the number of reconstructed candidates,
raising the probability of overlapping signatures and ambiguous associations. Dense
final states, such as the cores of high-pT jets or boosted heavy-particle decays, can
produce nearby tracks and merged detector signals that violate the assumptions used
by standard reconstruction algorithms. In these regimes, the relevant information is
often distributed across many correlated measurements rather than contained in a
single variable.

Machine learning provides a complementary approach in which these correlations
are learned directly from data. Rather than specifying all decision boundaries by
hand, learned models can exploit high-dimensional patterns that are di!cult to encode
explicitly, while retaining the goal of conventional reconstruction: to infer a compact
and physically meaningful description of the event.

4.4.3 Representations of Collider Events

The input representation is central to the e"ective use of machine learning in object
reconstruction [81–83]. Collider events are not naturally described by a single fixed-size
vector, but by variable-size collections of detector measurements and reconstructed
objects, such as tracking hits, calorimeter clusters, tracks associated with a jet, and
physics objects in the event. Each element carries measured quantities, uncertainties,
and geometrical information, and the number of elements varies between events.

A compact representation can be obtained by reducing these collections to a fixed set
of high-level observables, such as vertex masses, jet-shape variables, or substructure
quantities. This approach is physically interpretable and has been widely used in
traditional multivariate classifiers, but it compresses the underlying detector information



Event Reconstruction 70

before learning is applied. Correlations between individual measurements may therefore
be lost.

Modern reconstruction models increasingly operate directly on lower-level collections.
The input can be written schematically as a set

X = {x1, . . . , xN}, (4.8)

where each element xi represents a constituent such as a detector hit, cluster, or
reconstructed object. In many cases, the ordering of these elements is not physically
meaningful, and the model should not treat an arbitrary storage order as part of the
event description. Architectures for collider data must therefore either operate on the
collection without relying on an ordering, or use an ordering whose physical motivation
is explicit.

Many reconstruction tasks depend on correlations between elements [84–86]. Hits from
the same charged particle form a coherent trajectory, tracks from a heavy-flavour decay
may be compatible with a common displaced vertex, and constituents of a boosted
jet encode the decay structure of the parent particle. Graph neural networks and
transformer architectures [87] can both be viewed as relational models for updating
element representations through information exchange with other elements. They di"er
primarily in how the interaction structure is defined. In graph-based models, elements
are represented as nodes and messages are exchanged along edges. These message-
passing operations may themselves use attention weights to determine the relative
importance of neighbouring nodes. In transformer-based models, interactions between
elements are defined directly through the attention mechanism. Both approaches can
respect the variable-size structure of collider data while learning correlations between
detector measurements or reconstructed objects.

Machine learning can then be used either for object identification or for structured
prediction. In object identification, the reconstruction chain has already produced a
candidate object, and the model assigns it a label or probability. Examples include
electron and photon identification, pile-up rejection, and flavour tagging [71, 73, 77, 88].
In structured prediction, the model must infer relationships or assignments between
detector measurements, as in hit-to-track assignment, vertex finding, or particle-flow-
style reconstruction [89,90]. These tasks are closer to reconstruction itself, since the
output may be a partition of detector measurements, a set of associations between



Event Reconstruction 71

low-level and high-level objects, or a variable-size collection of reconstructed candidates.
The desired output is therefore not a single label, but a set of objects, each associated
with a subset of the inputs. The tracking studies presented in Chapters 6 and 7 use
structured prediction to infer candidate trajectories and hit-assignment masks directly
from detector hits.

model correlations between elements of a variable-size event representation. In collider
applications these elements may be detector hits, calorimeter clusters, reconstructed
tracks, jet constituents, or higher-level physics objects. The relevant information is
often relational: hits must be associated into trajectories, tracks may be compatible
with a common displaced vertex, and jet constituents may encode the decay structure
of a heavy particle. Attention-based architectures provide a flexible mechanism for
learning such relationships directly from the data.

Chapter 5

Tracking Challenges in Dense High-pT

Heavy-Flavour Environments

This chapter examines charged-particle tracking in dense detector environments, with
a particular focus on charged particles from high-pT b-hadron decays. These topologies
combine high local track density with displaced trajectories, producing ambiguous hit
associations that are challenging for conventional sequential ATLAS track reconstruc-
tion [56].

The purpose of the chapter is diagnostic. Simulated boosted Z
→ and single-b-hadron

samples are used to test whether the observed high-pT e!ciency loss is driven by the
displaced decay topology alone or by the surrounding dense jet environment. The
loss is then localised approximately within the conventional reconstruction chain, and
track-finding diagnostics are used to test whether it can be recovered through local
modifications of the existing reconstruction procedure. The results motivate the learned
hit-association methods developed in Chapters 6 and 7.

5.1 Track Reconstruction Challenges in Dense
Environments

Charged-particle tracking underpins much of the ATLAS event-reconstruction chain, as
introduced in Section 4.2. Tracks are used to reconstruct interaction vertices, associate
charged particles with jets and leptons, mitigate pile-up, and identify displaced decay

76



Tracking Challenges in Dense High-pT Heavy-Flavour Environments 77

signatures. Good tracking performance is therefore essential for the physics objects
and selections used in precision measurements and searches.

This is especially important for heavy-flavour reconstruction. As discussed in Sec-
tion 4.3.3, bottom hadrons travel a measurable distance before decaying, producing
charged particles with non-zero impact parameters relative to the primary vertex.
Reconstructing these displaced tracks provides the main experimental handle for iden-
tifying jets containing b-hadrons. Tracking ine!ciencies for b-hadron decay products
can therefore degrade heavy-flavour tagging performance, a"ecting analyses involving
top quarks, Higgs bosons, and other heavy particles.

Tracking becomes more di!cult in dense detector environments. These arise globally
from pile-up interactions and locally in the cores of high-pT jets, where many charged
particles are produced within a small angular region. Both are central to the LHC
physics programme. High pile-up is an unavoidable consequence of increasing instanta-
neous luminosity and will become more severe at the HL-LHC [50], while high-pT jets
are central to boosted heavy-particle reconstruction and searches for new resonances.

In dense environments, the increased density of charged-particle trajectories raises the
detector occupancy and the probability that hits or clusters from distinct particles
overlap. During seed finding and track extension, several space-points may be compati-
ble with a given track hypothesis, increasing the number of candidate trajectories. As
discussed in Section 4.2, conventional tracking algorithms control this combinatorial
growth by imposing constraints at each stage of the reconstruction chain. These
requirements are essential for robust tracking in generic collision events, but their
optimisation involves a trade-o" between reconstruction e!ciency, fake-track rejection,
and computational cost.

A related di!culty is hit sharing and cluster overlap. When charged particles traverse
nearby regions of the silicon sensors, their charge deposits can merge into a single
reconstructed cluster. Such merged clusters no longer have a one-to-one correspondence
with charged-particle trajectories, as illustrated in Figure 5.1. Shared or ambiguous
measurements are therefore a genuine feature of dense topologies, rather than simply
a reconstruction defect. Algorithms must decide whether to assign a measurement
to multiple track candidates, split the corresponding cluster, or reject one of the
candidates.



Tracking Challenges in Dense High-pT Heavy-Flavour Environments 78

a Single-particle pixel clusters. b Merged clusters from multiple particles.

Figure 5.1: Illustration of pixel cluster formation in the silicon detector [62]. Overlapping

These e"ects coincide in the reconstruction of charged particles from high-pT b-hadron
decays. As the momentum of the parent hadron increases, its decay products become
increasingly collimated. Several physically correlated charged particles can therefore be
produced away from the primary vertex while traversing nearby regions of the silicon
detector. This topology combines displacement with high local track density, increasing
cluster merging, hit sharing, and combinatorial ambiguity between track candidates. It
is therefore challenging for conventional track reconstruction algorithms, which proceed
through a sequence of seed formation, track finding, and ambiguity-resolution steps [56].

5.2.2 Single-b-Hadron Samples

A dedicated set of single-b-hadron samples is used as a control sample. These samples

resulting events contain the charged decay products of a single b-hadron, rather than a
full hadronic jet environment. The samples are processed through the same detector-

→ samples.

The single-b-hadron sample is therefore used as a diagnostic control rather than as a
physical model of a jet with the surrounding activity removed. It isolates the displaced

5.3 Localisation of E!ciency Losses

Previous studies of dense high-pT heavy-flavour environments found that ambiguity res-
olution reduced the charged-particle reconstruction e!ciency for tracks from b-hadron
decays by approximately 40% at the highest b-hadron transverse momenta consid-
ered [102]. Many tracks were found by the pattern-recognition stage but subsequently
rejected by the ambiguity solver, with the loss increasing with b-hadron transverse mo-
mentum. The principal rejection mechanisms were an excessive number of shared silicon
hits, too few total or unique silicon hits, and the prior acceptance of a higher-scoring
candidate using the same measurements. These requirements are interdependent, for
example, removing shared measurements can cause a candidate to fail the minimum-hit
requirements, while accepting one candidate changes the number of measurements
available uniquely to candidates processed later. Consequently, relaxing an individual
ambiguity-solver requirement provided only limited recovery, since candidates could
instead fail another part of the selection.

These observations motivate two diagnostic questions. First, is the reduced e!ciency
primarily a consequence of the displaced b-hadron decay topology itself, or of the dense
jet environment in which such decays occur? Second, where in the earlier reconstruction
chain does the e!ciency loss arise?

The first question is tested by comparing the reconstruction e!ciency in the boosted
Z

→ and single-b-hadron samples introduced in Section 5.2. The boosted Z

while the single-b-hadron samples provide an isolated displaced-decay topology without
the surrounding charged-particle activity of a realistic jet.

with the surrounding dense charged-particle environment.

5.4 Diagnostic Ablations

The stage-by-stage localisation in Section 5.3 motivates a closer examination of track
finding. In the standard ATLAS reconstruction chain, accepted seeds are extrapolated
through the tracking volume, compatible detector elements are collected into a search
road, and track candidates are built by a combinatorial Kalman filter that incrementally
associates silicon measurements with the evolving trajectory [56]. Diagnostic and
ablation studies were therefore performed to test whether the observed loss could be
associated with a specific configurable requirement in this procedure.

The studies used the boosted Z
→ samples introduced in Section 5.2.1, together with ad-

ditional instrumentation of the track maker. Silicon-cluster truth links were propagated
to space-points and seeds, allowing each seed to be associated with a parent b-hadron
where possible. A seed was classified as originating from a b-hadron only when all three
constituent space-points were truth matched to the same charged particle originating
from a b-hadron. The subsequent track-maker outcome was then recorded for these
truth-identified b-hadron seeds.

The diagnostic study compared the track-maker outcomes for an inclusive sample of
truth-identified b-hadron seeds with those for seeds associated with parent b-hadrons
satisfying pT → 500 GeV. Summary counters assigned seeds to broad outcomes, includ-
ing failure to estimate initial track parameters, an insu!cient detector-element road,
failure to form an accepted track candidate, rejection by the candidate-overlap veto,
and duplicate removal. In the high-pT sample, approximately 34% of truth-identified
b-hadron seeds were assigned to the broad cannot find track category, compared with
17% in the inclusive sample. The fraction assigned to the candidate-overlap veto
category also increased, from approximately 4% to 10%. The cannot find track category



Tracking Challenges in Dense High-pT Heavy-Flavour Environments 86

contains several stages of candidate construction, including hit- and quality-based re-
quirements applied after combinatorial track building. These results therefore localised
the dominant loss to candidate formation and competition during track finding, but
did not identify a unique algorithmic decision responsible for the ine!ciency.

Further instrumentation showed that a substantial fraction of the losses within cannot
find track were associated with requirements depending on the minimum number of
silicon clusters, nmin

clus. An ablation was therefore performed in which this requirement
was reduced from 8 to 5. This recovered approximately 75% of the seeds previously
rejected during candidate formation. However, the recovery did not translate into a
corresponding increase in either the SiSP-seeded or final reconstructed-track e!ciencies.
Instead, many of the recovered candidates were rejected at later stages, particularly by
the not new track overlap requirement. Disabling this requirement in combination with
the reduced cluster cut produced only a small additional gain, with losses migrating
into other residual categories.

These results illustrate why the ine!ciency is di!cult to recover through individual
local modifications of the conventional reconstruction chain. Track finding consists of a
sequence of coupled decisions, including seed initialisation, detector-road construction,
combinatorial extension, hit selection, candidate pruning, quality requirements, and
overlap handling. Changing one requirement modifies the population of candidates
reaching later decisions, so an apparent recovery from one rejection category can
reappear as a rejection elsewhere or produce candidates that do not survive the final
hit-content and truth-matching requirements.

5.5 Conclusion

This chapter has examined charged-particle reconstruction in dense detector envi-
ronments, with a particular focus on particles produced in high-pT b-hadron decays.
These topologies combine displaced trajectories with high local charged-particle density,
leading to cluster overlap, hit sharing, and combinatorial ambiguity between candidate
tracks. They therefore provide a stringent test of the standard ATLAS reconstruction
chain.

The studies demonstrated that the reduced reconstruction e!ciency observed at high
b-hadron transverse momentum is primarily associated with the dense jet environment



Tracking Challenges in Dense High-pT Heavy-Flavour Environments 87

rather than with the displaced decay topology alone. The loss is distributed across
the reconstruction chain, with seed formation contributing only a small fraction, while
substantial losses occur during both track finding and ambiguity resolution. Targeted
track-finding ablations did not isolate a single configurable source of the ine!ciency,
nor did they recover the lost reconstructed tracks.

These results illustrate the di!culty of recovering e!ciency through local modifications
of the conventional reconstruction chain. Track reconstruction is sequential and highly
coupled. Changes to seed extension, track-candidate requirements, overlap handling, or
ambiguity resolution alter the candidate population reaching later stages. An apparent
recovery from one rejection category can therefore reappear as a rejection elsewhere.
Related ambiguity-resolution studies reached a similar conclusion, finding that high-pT

b-hadron tracks are often rejected by shared-hit and unique-hit requirements, and that
modifying individual ambiguity-solver selections gives only limited recovery [102].

These studies of dense high-pT heavy-flavour topologies therefore expose practical
limitations of a sequential reconstruction procedure based on hand-engineered candi-
date formation and rejection stages. These limitations motivate the investigation of
alternative reconstruction formulations based on learned detector-hit association. The
following chapters study such a formulation in the TrackML detector setting, without
presenting it as a demonstrated solution to the specific ATLAS ine!ciencies identified
here.



Chapter 6

Transformers for Charged-Particle

Track Reconstruction

This chapter presents a Transformer-based approach to charged-particle track recon-
struction using a MaskFormer-inspired architecture [87, 93, 94]. Tracking is formulated
as a set-prediction problem in which a fixed set of decoder queries represents candidate
charged-particle trajectories, and the model predicts hit-assignment masks directly
from detector hits.

The study is performed on the TrackML dataset [103], a simplified benchmark de-
signed to capture key features of high-occupancy silicon tracking at the HL-LHC. The
chapter aims to determine whether a fixed-query Transformer decoder can perform
high-e!ciency hit-to-track assignment in a simplified HL-LHC-like tracking environ-
ment. The resulting models establish a baseline for query-based Transformer tracking.
Targeted architectural and training optimisations are then used to strengthen this
fixed-query baseline and define the reference model for the scale-up studies in Chapter 7.

Figure 6.1 provides an overview of the reconstruction architecture developed in this
chapter. The model comprises two sequential stages. First, a Transformer-based hit-
filtering network operates on the full detector-hit collection and predicts whether each
hit is associated with the target reconstructable-particle population. Only hits passing
this selection are retained, substantially reducing the input multiplicity presented to
the track-reconstruction model. In both stages, hits are mapped to learned embeddings
and processed by Transformer encoders using local self-attention over hits ordered in
azimuthal angle ↽.

88



Transformers for Charged-Particle Track Reconstruction 89

The second stage formulates track reconstruction as query-based set prediction. A fixed
collection of learned object queries provides latent candidate-track representations,
which are iteratively refined by a Transformer decoder through query self-attention and
bidirectional query–hit cross-attention. For each query, the final representations are
used to predict whether the candidate corresponds to a physical trajectory, which filtered
hits belong to that trajectory, and approximate particle-level parameters. The hit-
assignment masks are predicted jointly from the refined query and hit embeddings, while
the candidate-validity and track-parameter predictions are obtained from the refined
query representations. The architecture thereby predicts complete track candidates
directly from the detector-hit collection, without first constructing an explicit graph of
candidate hit–hit connections.
